BUCCA.name: Bucca (Vir Rōmānus)
BUCCA.design: A huge, loud woman in her forties who runs a street cookshop in ancient Rome: booming, warm, raspy chest voice, bossy, quick and funny. Speaks English with a light Italian accent (never American).
BUCCA.sample: Sausages! Hot sausages! One coin! What do you want? Do you want food? The cabbages are good. Be quiet, Bibulus, I am talking!

PORC.name: Porcellus (Vir Rōmānus)
PORC.design: A cheeky, greedy, loud young man with a high, boyish, slightly nasal voice: bright, always excited, often with his mouth full. Speaks English with a light Italian accent (never American).
PORC.sample: I am the emperor! Marcus, am I bigger than you? I think about sausages. I always think. Give me the sausage, please! Oink!

MARCUS.name: Marcus (Vir Rōmānus)
MARCUS.design: A serious, calm, very polite young man with a light, clear, boyish voice: precise, gentle and thoughtful, old for his years. Speaks English with a light Italian accent (never American).
MARCUS.sample: I am reading. The book is about philosophy. A philosopher is a man who thinks, a man who looks for the truth. I will not ride without a reason.

BIBULUS.name: Bibulus (Vir Rōmānus)
BIBULUS.design: A lazy old drunk man in his sixties: hoarse, slow, slurred and sleepy, gravelly, deadpan. Speaks English with a light Italian accent (never American).
BIBULUS.sample: Mmmph. What is this? Water? I would rather die. I am the emperor of wine. Bucca, I want to tell you something... Nothing. I know nothing.

PRIMUS.name: Primus (Vir Rōmānus)
PRIMUS.design: A pompous, theatrical middle-aged man who thinks he is a great prophet: rich booming baritone, grand and dramatic. Speaks English with a light Italian accent (never American).
PRIMUS.sample: Look! A new star! Today on this hill a king is born! O king! O future emperor! Look, gold! All kings smell, woman. All of them.

SECUNDUS.name: Secundus (Vir Rōmānus)
SECUNDUS.design: A fat, practical, slightly whiny middle-aged man: nasal tenor voice, sceptical and dry. Speaks English with a light Italian accent (never American).
SECUNDUS.sample: Where? The sky is big, Primus. Where in the sky? Which of the two houses? It is the smell of cabbages. And of pigs. Surely not.

TERTIUS.name: Tertius (Vir Rōmānus)
TERTIUS.design: A tiny, very old man who is nearly deaf and nearly blind: thin, high, quavering, confused and sweet. Speaks English with a light Italian accent (never American).
TERTIUS.sample: What is it? Is it the moon? Oh! Who is hitting me? The wall is rude. Is the dog the king? Oh. Kind people. Where is the world?

MONK.name: Frater Ignotus (Vir Rōmānus)
MONK.design: A grumpy elderly English monk in a cold medieval monastery: dry, low, weary and deadpan, a sarcastic murmur. British English accent (never American).
MONK.sample: I am Brother Unknown. The year is eleven fifty. The monastery is cold. The ink is cold. My fingers are cold. The abbot says: write this book. I write.

SABIDIUS.name: Sabidius (Vir Rōmānus)
SABIDIUS.design: A lazy, smug, elderly Greek philosopher who is a useless slave: soft, slow, silky, superior and unbothered. Speaks English with a Greek accent (never American).
SABIDIUS.sample: You buy my body. You do not buy my mind. My mind is free. My mind does not cut cabbages. Work is patient. Work waits. I am a philosopher.

HADRIAN.name: Hadrian (Vir Rōmānus)
HADRIAN.design: A commanding Roman emperor in his fifties: deep, warm, authoritative, amused, a rich and slow voice. Speaks English with a light Italian accent (never American).
HADRIAN.sample: Hello, Marcus! This horse is yours. Ha! Listen to him! You are not Verus, Marcus. You are Verissimus! And who are you, little one?

PLAGOSUS.name: Plagosus (Vir Rōmānus)
PLAGOSUS.design: A small, bald, furious schoolmaster: sharp, barking, nasal, shouting and strict. Speaks English with a light Italian accent (never American).
PLAGOSUS.sample: A new pupil! What is your name? Do you know your letters? Not even A? In my school nobody laughs. In my school everybody learns. Or hurts.

PARROT.name: Psittacus (Vir Rōmānus)
PARROT.design: A shrill, squawky cartoon parrot: high, scratchy, screeching, fast, repeating words, very comic. Not American.
PARROT.sample: Hello! Hello! Stupid Bucca! Stupid Bucca! Emperor! Emperor! Sausage! Sausage! When do we get to Rome? When do we get to Rome?

MAN1.name: Romanus (Vir Rōmānus)
MAN1.design: A gruff working-class man in his forties from ancient Rome: rough, tired, impatient, deep. Speaks English with a light Italian accent (never American).
MAN1.sample: What do you want? Here nobody is born. Go away, or the dog comes! The best slaves! Buy, citizens! Dinner is three coins. Here you pay.

title: Pars I · Capitula 1–8 · Latin only (× 1)
summary: Vir Rōmānus, Part I, all eight chapters in one track: the whole story in Latin only, once, from the stupid star (121 AD) to the play (134 AD). Full cast; narrator Iulia (Rossana).

items.en: Vir Rōmānus. Chapter one: The stupid star.
Prologue: what will happen?

In this chapter it is night in Rome. Three astrologers see a new star. The star leads them to the Caelian hill, where there are two houses: a big house and a dirty cookshop. The astrologers are looking for a king. Whom will they find? A pig? A baby? Both?
items.la: In hōc capitulō Rōma est nocte. Trēs astrologī stēllam novam vident. Stēlla eōs ad montem Caelium dūcit, ubi duae domūs sunt: domus magna et popīna sordida. Astrologī rēgem quaerunt. Quem invenient? Porcum? Īnfantem? Ambōs?

items.en: Grammar: the nominative (who?), one and many (porcus, porcī), est and sunt, and questions (-ne, num, quis, quid).
items.la: Grammatica: nōminātīvus (quis?), ūnus et multī (porcus, porcī), est et sunt, et quaestiōnēs (-ne, num, quis, quid).

items.en: Grammar.

Hello, reader! This is a Latin book. In this chapter one thing is big: who? Who is in the street? A pig is in the street. "Porcus" is the nominative: the one who is, the one who acts, the one who smells.
items.la: Salvē, lēctor! Hic est liber Latīnus. In hōc capitulō ūna rēs est magna: quis? Quis est in viā? Porcus est in viā. "Porcus" est nōminātīvus: is quī est, is quī agit, is quī olet.

items.en: One pig, many pigs. One star, many stars. One egg, many eggs. A pig alone is sad. Many pigs are happy. And they smell.
items.la: Ūnus porcus, multī porcī. Ūna stēlla, multae stēllae. Ūnum ōvum, multa ōva. Porcus sōlus est trīstis. Porcī multī sunt laetī. Et olent.
ūnus, ūna, ūnum — multī, multae, multa

items.en: Est = one. Sunt = many. "The astrologer is stupid." "The astrologers are stupid." This is not grammar. This is the truth.
items.la: Est = ūnus. Sunt = multī. "Astrologus est stultus." "Astrologī sunt stultī." Hoc nōn est grammatica. Hoc est vēritās.

items.en: Questions. -ne at the end of a word: "Is the pig a king?" Num expects "no": "Surely the pig is not a king?" — "No!" Quis? = a person. Quid? = a thing.
items.la: Quaestiōnēs. -ne in fīne verbī: "Estne porcus rēx?" Num exspectat "nōn": "Num porcus est rēx?" — "Minimē!" Quis? = persōna. Quid? = rēs.

items.en: "Who is in the kitchen?" — "Bucca." "What is in the pot?" — "Nobody knows. Not even Bucca."
items.la: "Quis est in culīnā?" — "Bucca." "Quid est in ollā?" — "Nēmō scit. Nē Bucca quidem."

Reading one: Night.
It is night. Three astrologers follow a star, but the star is stupid.
items.la: Nox est. Trēs astrologī stēllam sequuntur, sed stēlla est stulta.

items.en: Rome is a big city. In the city there are seven hills. One hill is the Caelian.
items.la: Rōma est urbs magna. In urbe sunt septem montēs. Ūnus mōns est Caelius.

items.en: On the Caelian hill there are two houses. The first house is big and beautiful. It is the house of Annius Verus, a noble and rich man.
items.la: In monte Caeliō sunt duae domūs. Domus prīma est magna et pulchra. Est domus Annī Vērī, virī nōbilis et dīvitis.

items.en: In the garden there are roses, statues, slaves.
items.la: In hortō sunt rosae, statuae, servī.

items.en: The second house is not really a house. It is a cookshop: small, dirty, full of smoke.
items.la: Domus secunda nōn est vērē domus. Est popīna: parva, sordida, plēna fūmī.

items.en: The cookshop is Bucca's. Bucca is a cook. Bucca is a huge woman. Bucca's voice is huge.
items.la: Popīna est Buccae. Bucca est coqua. Bucca est fēmina ingēns. Vōx Buccae est ingēns.

items.en: Bucca's nose is huge. In the cookshop nothing is small, except the money.
items.la: Nāsus Buccae est ingēns. In popīnā nihil est parvum, nisi pecūnia.

items.en: Behind the cookshop is a pig pen. In the pig pen there are pigs. The pigs are many, fat, happy.
items.la: Post popīnam est hara. In harā sunt porcī. Porcī sunt multī, crassī, laetī.

items.en: The pigs are not noble. The pigs are not rich. But the pigs are happier than Annius Verus.
items.la: Porcī nōn sunt nōbilēs. Porcī nōn sunt dīvitēs. Sed porcī sunt laetiōrēs quam Annius Vērus.

items.en: It is night. The sky is black. In the sky there are many stars. But one star is new.
items.la: Nox est. Caelum est nigrum. In caelō sunt multae stēllae. Sed ūna stēlla est nova.

items.en: The new star is bright and big, and it walks across the sky. Stars do not walk.
items.la: Stēlla nova est clāra et magna, et ambulat per caelum. Stēllae nōn ambulant.

items.en: This star walks. It is a stupid star.
items.la: Haec stēlla ambulat. Est stēlla stulta.

items.en: In the street there are three men. The men are astrologers. Primus is tall. Secundus is fat.
items.la: In viā sunt trēs virī. Virī sunt astrologī. Prīmus est longus. Secundus est crassus.

items.en: Tertius is small and old, and he does not see well, and he does not hear well.
items.la: Tertius est parvus et vetus, et nōn bene videt, et nōn bene audit.

items.en: Look! A new star!
Where?
There! In the sky!
The sky is big, Primus. Where in the sky?
items.la: Caelum est magnum, Prīme. Ubi in caelō?

items.en: There! Above the Caelian hill!
What is it? Is it the moon?
No, Tertius. It is not the moon. It is a star. A new star is a sign. Today on this hill a king is born.
items.la: Minimē, Tertī. Nōn est lūna. Est stēlla. Stēlla nova est signum. Hodiē in hōc monte nāscitur rēx.

items.en: The ruler of the world is born!
Where is the world?
Everywhere, Tertius. The world is everywhere.
Oh. It is big.
The astrologers follow the star. The star walks, the astrologers walk. The star stops, the astrologers stop.
items.la: Astrologī stēllam sequuntur. Stēlla ambulat, astrologī ambulant. Stēlla cōnsistit, astrologī cōnsistunt.

items.en: Tertius does not stop. Tertius walks into a wall.
items.la: Tertius nōn cōnsistit. Tertius in mūrum ambulat.

items.en: Oh! Who is hitting me?
The wall, Tertius.
The wall is rude.
Now the star stands above the two houses: not above the big house, not above the cookshop, but between the houses.
items.la: Nunc stēlla stat suprā duās domūs: nōn suprā domum magnam, nōn suprā popīnam, sed inter domūs.

items.en: The star is stupid. The astrologers are stupider.
items.la: Stēlla est stulta. Astrologī sunt stultiōrēs.

items.en: Which of the two? The big house or the cookshop?
It is easy. The big house is beautiful. A ruler is born in a beautiful house.
items.la: Facile est. Domus magna est pulchra. Imperātor in domō pulchrā nāscitur.

items.en: Primus knocks on the door of the big house. The door opens. In the doorway is a slave.
items.la: Prīmus iānuam domūs magnae pulsat. Iānua aperītur. In iānuā est servus.

items.en: The slave is tired and angry, because it is night.
items.la: Servus est fessus et īrātus, quia nox est.

items.en: What do you want?
Hello! We are astrologers. Here a king is born!
items.la: Salvē! Nōs sumus astrologī. Hīc nāscitur rēx!

items.en: Here nobody is born. Go away!
But the star...
The star is not mine. Go away, or the dog comes.
items.la: Stēlla nōn est mea. Abīte, aut canis venit.

items.en: A dog? Is the dog the king?
The door is shut. From the big house comes a shout. The astrologers do not hear. From the cookshop comes a smell.
items.la: Iānua clauditur. Ex domō magnā venit clāmor. Astrologī nōn audiunt. Ex popīnā venit odor.

items.en: The astrologers sniff.
What is this smell? Is it the smell of a king?
items.la: Quid est hic odor? Estne odor rēgis?

items.en: It is the smell of cabbages. And of pigs.
Good! Kings are pigs. Everybody knows.
items.la: Bene! Rēgēs sunt porcī. Omnēs sciunt.

items.en: Excursus: Rome in the year 121. True!
items.la: Excursus: Rōma annō centēsimō vīcēsimō prīmō. Vērum!

items.en: Who is emperor in 121? And why does he have a beard?
items.la: Quis est imperātor annō centēsimō vīcēsimō prīmō? Et cūr barbam habet?

items.en: This is true. In the year 121 the Roman emperor is Hadrian. But Hadrian is not in Rome.
items.la: Hoc est vērum. Annō centēsimō vīcēsimō prīmō imperātor Rōmānus est Hadriānus. Sed Hadriānus nōn est Rōmae.

items.en: Hadrian is always on a journey: in Gaul, in Britain, in Greece, in Egypt.
items.la: Hadriānus semper est in itinere: in Galliā, in Britanniā, in Graeciā, in Aegyptō.

items.en: Hadrian wants to see his empire, and the Romans never see their emperor.
items.la: Hadriānus imperium suum vidēre vult, et Rōmānī imperātōrem suum numquam vident.

items.en: Hadrian has a beard. The emperors before him do not have a beard. Hadrian is the first emperor with a beard.
items.la: Hadriānus barbam habet. Imperātōrēs priōrēs barbam nōn habent. Hadriānus est prīmus imperātor cum barbā.

items.en: Why? The Historia Augusta says: on Hadrian's face there are blemishes, and the beard covers the blemishes.
items.la: Cūr? Historia Augusta dīcit: in faciē Hadriānī sunt vitia, et barba vitia tegit.

items.en: A beard is like a tunic for the face.
In Rome there are perhaps a million people. Many are poor. Many live in "islands": tall houses, dirty, full of mice.
items.la: Rōmae sunt fortasse mīlle mīlia hominum. Multī sunt pauperēs. Multī habitant in īnsulīs: domūs altae, sordidae, plēnae mūrium.

items.en: A Roman "island" is not an island in the sea. It is a big, bad house. If an island burns, many die.
items.la: Īnsula Rōmāna nōn est īnsula in marī. Est domus magna et mala. Sī īnsula ārdet, multī moriuntur.

items.en: If an island falls down, more die. If an island stands, everybody complains.
items.la: Sī īnsula cadit, plūrēs moriuntur. Sī īnsula stat, omnēs queruntur.

items.en: The Romans do not have numbers for years. They do not say "the year 121". The Romans say: "the year in which Annius Verus, for the second time, and Augur are consuls".
items.la: Rōmānī numerōs annōrum nōn habent. "Annus centēsimus vīcēsimus prīmus" nōn dīcunt. Rōmānī dīcunt: "annus, quō Annius Vērus iterum et Augur sunt cōnsulēs".

items.en: This is long. The Romans are patient.
items.la: Hoc est longum. Rōmānī sunt patientēs.

items.en: Reading two: A baby in the pig pen.
The astrologers enter the cookshop. In the pig pen, something is shouting.
items.la: Astrologī popīnam intrant. In harā aliquid clāmat.

items.en: In the cookshop is Bucca. Bucca is cooking cabbages. On a table sleeps Bibulus. Bibulus is a poor and dirty man.
items.la: In popīnā est Bucca. Bucca caulēs coquit. In mēnsā dormit Bibulus. Bibulus est vir pauper et sordidus.

items.en: Bibulus is always in the cookshop. Bibulus always sleeps. When Bibulus does not sleep, Bibulus drinks.
items.la: Bibulus semper in popīnā est. Bibulus semper dormit. Quandō Bibulus nōn dormit, Bibulus bibit.

items.en: The door of the cookshop opens. In come three astrologers.
items.la: Iānua popīnae aperītur. Intrant trēs astrologī.

items.en: Hello, o woman! Where is the king?
items.la: Salvē, ō fēmina! Ubi est rēx?

items.en: King? Here there is no king. Here is a cookshop. Here there are food, wine and Bibulus.
items.la: Rēx? Hīc nōn est rēx. Hīc est popīna. Hīc sunt cibus, vīnum et Bibulus.

items.en: Mmmph.
Is that man the king?
Him? That is Bibulus. Bibulus is not a king. Bibulus is a pig.
items.la: Ille? Ille est Bibulus. Bibulus nōn est rēx. Bibulus est porcus.

items.en: A pig! Look! A sign!
What do you want? Do you want food? The cabbages are good. Today there are cabbages. Yesterday there were cabbages. Tomorrow there will be cabbages.
items.la: Quid vultis? Cibumne vultis? Caulēs sunt bonī. Hodiē caulēs sunt. Herī caulēs erant. Crās caulēs erunt.

items.en: We are not looking for food. We are looking for a king. The star...
items.la: Nōn cibum quaerimus. Rēgem quaerimus. Stēlla…

items.en: Suddenly from the pig pen comes a small voice: "Waaah!" Everyone goes quiet. Even Bibulus goes quiet, but Bibulus is always quiet.
items.la: Subitō ex harā venit vōx parva: "Uāāāh!" Omnēs tacent. Etiam Bibulus tacet, sed Bibulus semper tacet.

items.en: What is that? Pigs do not shout like that.
items.la: Quid est? Porcī nōn sīc clāmant.

items.en: Bucca runs into the pig pen. The astrologers run after Bucca. Tertius runs into the door.
items.la: Bucca in haram currit. Astrologī post Buccam currunt. Tertius in iānuam currit.

items.en: In the pig pen, among the pigs, there is a basket. In the basket there is a baby. The baby is naked, red, fat.
items.la: In harā, inter porcōs, est corbis. In corbe est īnfāns. Īnfāns est nūdus, rubicundus, crassus.

items.en: The baby does not cry; the baby laughs. Piglets sit around the basket. The baby is like a piglet.
items.la: Īnfāns nōn plōrat; īnfāns cachinnat. Porcellī circum corbem sedent. Īnfāns est similis porcellō.

items.en: The piglet is like the baby. Who is the piglet? Who is the baby? Nobody knows.
items.la: Porcellus est similis īnfantī. Quis est porcellus? Quis est īnfāns? Nēmō scit.

items.en: Who are you, little one? Who leaves you here?
items.la: Quis es tū, parve? Quis tē hīc relinquit?

items.en: Oink.
Oh! You are a piglet! Good. You are Porcellus, Piglet.
items.la: Ō! Porcellus es! Bene. Tū es Porcellus.

items.en: Look! The star is above the pig pen! This is the king!
items.la: Ecce! Stēlla est suprā haram! Hic est rēx!

items.en: A king in a pig pen? Surely a king is not born in a pig pen?
items.la: Rēx in harā? Num rēx in harā nāscitur?

items.en: Why not? At this time all things are new.
items.la: Cūr nōn? Hōc tempore omnia sunt nova.

items.en: The astrologers kneel. In the dung. Dung is everywhere.
items.la: Astrologī genua flectunt. In stercore. Stercus est ubīque.

items.en: O king! O future emperor! Look, gold!
items.la: Ō rēx! Ō imperātor futūre! Ecce, aurum!

items.en: Gold! Excellent!
Bucca bites the coin. The coin is real.
items.la: Bucca nummum mordet. Nummus est vērus.

items.en: O king! Look, a book of the stars!
A book? I cannot read. But a book burns well. Thanks!
items.la: Liber? Ego legere nōn possum. Sed liber ārdet bene. Grātiās!

items.en: O king! Look, fish sauce!
What?
Garum. Garum is good. Garum is made from rotten fish.
items.la: Garum. Garum est bonum. Garum est ex piscibus putridīs.

items.en: I have garum. In a cookshop there is always garum.
items.la: Garum habeō. In popīnā semper est garum.

items.en: Oh.
Woman! This baby is the future emperor! King of the world! Lord of the lands!
items.la: Fēmina! Hic īnfāns est imperātor futūrus! Rēx mundī! Dominus terrārum!

items.en: This one? This one is a piglet. This one smells.
items.la: Hic? Hic est porcellus. Hic olet.

items.en: All kings smell.
A real Latin text: Historia Augusta, Vīta Marcī 1.5.
items.la: Textus vērus: Historia Augusta, Vīta Marcī.

items.en: A real book about Marcus: where and when was he born?
items.la: Liber vērus dē Marcō: ubi et quandō nātus est?

items.en: Brother Unknown (see the margin) has another book: the Historia Augusta.
items.la: Frāter Ignōtus (vidē marginem) alium librum habet: Historiam Augustam.

items.en: There it is written: Marcus was born in Rome, on the Caelian hill, in the gardens. The day is the sixth before the Kalends of May: that is, the twenty-sixth of April.
items.la: Ibi scrīptum est: Marcus nātus est Rōmae, in monte Caeliō, in hortīs. Diēs est sextus ante Kalendās Māiās: id est, vīcēsimus sextus Aprīlis.

items.en: The consuls are Marcus's grandfather (for the second time) and a man who is called "Augur".
items.la: Cōnsulēs sunt avus Marcī (iterum) et vir quī "Augur" vocātur.

items.en: The real text.
Marcus was born in Rome on the sixth day before the Kalends of May, on the Caelian hill, in the gardens, when his grandfather, for the second time, and Augur were consuls.
items.la: Natus est Marcus Romae ante diem sextum Kalendās Māiās in monte Caelio in hortis avo suo iterum et Augure consulibus.

items.en: A real sentence from the Historia Augusta (Life of Marcus 1.5). Romans dated a day by counting back to the Kalends (the 1st) of the next month: "VI kl. Maias" = the 6th day before 1 May = 26 April. A year had no number: it was named by its two consuls, here in the ablative ("avo suo iterum et Augure consulibus" = "his grandfather (consul for the 2nd time) and Augur being consuls"). "In hortis" = in the gardens. In our story, the gardens have a cookshop and a pig pen next door. The Historia Augusta was written around 395 AD by one forger who pretends to be six writers. It mixes facts and lies. A perfect source for this book.
Reading three: Two babies.
The astrologers leave. Two babies lie in two houses.
items.la: Astrologī abeunt. Duo īnfantēs in duābus domibus iacent.

items.en: The astrologers go out. They are happy. They sing. Primus sings well, Secundus sings badly, Tertius sings a different song.
items.la: Astrologī exeunt. Laetī sunt. Cantant. Prīmus cantat bene, Secundus cantat male, Tertius cantat aliud carmen.

items.en: Then from the big house comes a great shout: "A son! A son is born! A son of Annius Verus! It is Marcus!" Slaves run.
items.la: Tunc ex domō magnā venit clāmor magnus: "Fīlius! Fīlius nātus est! Fīlius Annī Vērī! Marcus est!" Servī currunt.

items.en: Lamps burn. A dog barks.
What are they saying?
They are saying: "Farewell, most wise astrologers!"
Oh. Kind people.
The astrologers go away. The star goes away. The star too is tired.
items.la: Astrologī abeunt. Stēlla abit. Stēlla quoque est fessa.

items.en: In the cookshop Bucca looks at the baby. Bibulus wakes up.
items.la: In popīnā Bucca īnfantem spectat. Bibulus ēvigilat.

items.en: What is this?
This is Porcellus. The future emperor.
Ha! Emperor? This one? And I am an emperor. The emperor of wine.
items.la: Ha! Imperātor? Hic? Et ego sum imperātor. Imperātor vīnī.

items.en: Be quiet, Bibulus. The astrologers say...
Astrologers! Astrologers also say: "Tomorrow, rain." And tomorrow there is sun.
items.la: Astrologī! Astrologī quoque dīcunt: "Crās pluvia." Et crās est sōl.

items.en: Perhaps. But the gold is real. If this one is the emperor, gold will come. Much gold. Porcellus stays.
items.la: Fortasse. Sed aurum est vērum. Sī hic est imperātor, aurum veniet. Multum aurum. Porcellus manet.

items.en: And if he is not the emperor?
Then Porcellus works. In the kitchen. With the cabbages.
items.la: Tum Porcellus labōrat. In culīnā. Cum caulibus.

items.en: Oink.
In the big house, little Marcus lies in bed. Marcus does not cry. Marcus does not laugh.
items.la: In domō magnā, Marcus parvus in lectō iacet. Marcus nōn plōrat. Marcus nōn cachinnat.

items.en: Marcus is serious. Marcus thinks.
In the cookshop, little Porcellus lies in a basket. Porcellus does not think. Porcellus farts.
items.la: In popīnā, Porcellus parvus in corbe iacet. Porcellus nōn cōgitat. Porcellus pēdit.

items.en: The sound is big. The pigs are happy. Bibulus flees.
items.la: Sonus est magnus. Porcī laetī sunt. Bibulus fugit.

items.en: So begins the life of a Roman man. No, rather: of two men.
items.la: Sīc incipit vīta virī Rōmānī. Immō: duōrum virōrum.

items.en: In the margin: Brother Unknown.
Brother Unknown complains and quotes the Gospel.
items.la: Frāter Ignōtus queritur et Ēvangelium citat.

items.en: I am Brother Unknown. The year is 1150. The monastery is cold. The ink is cold.
items.la: Ego sum Frāter Ignōtus. Annus est mīllēsimus centēsimus quīnquāgēsimus. Mōnastērium est frīgidum. Ātrāmentum est frīgidum.

items.en: My fingers are cold. The abbot says: "Write this book." I write.
items.la: Digitī meī sunt frīgidī. Abbās dīcit: "Scrībe hunc librum." Ego scrībō.

items.en: But this book is stupid: astrologers, pigs, fish sauce.
items.la: Sed hic liber est stultus: astrologī, porcī, garum.

items.en: In the Gospel too there are men from the east and a star.
items.la: In Ēvangeliō quoque sunt virī ab oriente et stēlla.

items.en: Those men say: "Where is he who is born king of the Jews? For we have seen his star in the east and have come to adore him."
items.la: Illī virī dīcunt: "Ubi est, quī nātus est, rēx Iūdaeōrum? Vīdimus enim stēllam eius in oriente et vēnimus adōrāre eum.".

items.en: Those men are wise. These men are astrologers. There is a big difference.
items.la: Illī virī sunt sapientēs. Hī virī sunt astrologī. Magna differentia est.

items.en: And those men give gold, frankincense and myrrh. Not fish sauce.
items.la: Et illī virī dant aurum, tūs et myrrham. Nōn garum.

items.en: An old saying of scribes: "Three fingers write, the whole body works." It is true.
items.la: Vetus verbum scrīptōrum: "Trēs digitī scrībunt, tōtum corpus labōrat." Vērum est.

items.en: My back hurts.
Epilogue: what happened?

What happened? At night three astrologers saw a new star. The star led them to the Caelian hill. Prīmus knocked on the door of the big house, but a slave shouted: "Go away!" So the astrologers went into Bucca's cookshop.
items.la: Quid factum est? Nocte trēs astrologī stēllam novam vīdērunt. Stēlla eōs ad montem Caelium dūxit. Prīmus iānuam domūs magnae pulsāvit, sed servus clāmāvit: "Abīte!" Itaque astrologī popīnam Buccae intrāvērunt.

items.en: In the pig pen, among the pigs, they found a baby. They knelt and gave gifts: gold, a book, fish sauce. Bucca named the baby "Porcellus". That same night, in the big house, Marcus was born. Marcus thought. Porcellus farted.
items.la: In harā, inter porcōs, īnfantem invēnērunt. Genua flexērunt et dōna dedērunt: aurum, librum, garum. Bucca īnfantem "Porcellum" vocāvit. Eādem nocte, in domō magnā, Marcus nātus est. Marcus cōgitāvit. Porcellus pepēdit.

items.en: What next?

But who really is Porcellus? Where does he come from? And what will Bucca do with the astrologers' gold? Soon Porcellus will be four, and Bucca will go looking for the best fish sauce: in a town that no longer exists.
items.la: Sed quis est vērē Porcellus? Unde venit? Et quid faciet Bucca cum aurō astrologōrum? Mox Porcellus quattuor annōs habēbit, et Bucca garum optimum quaeret: in oppidō quod iam nōn est.

items.en: Vir Rōmānus. Chapter two: The Pompeii fish sauce.
Prologue: what will happen?

It is the year 125. Porcellus is four. Bucca has bad fish sauce and wants the best: Scaurus's fish sauce, from the town of Pompeii. But Bibulus knows something about Pompeii. Bucca, Porcellus and Bibulus make the trip. There they will find a clever man, and walls full of filthy words.
items.la: Annus est centēsimus vīcēsimus quīntus. Porcellus quattuor annōs habet. Bucca garum malum habet et garum optimum vult: garum Scaurī, ex oppidō Pompēiīs. Sed Bibulus aliquid dē Pompēiīs scit. Bucca, Porcellus et Bibulus iter faciunt. Ibi virum callidum invenient, et mūrōs plēnōs verbōrum foedōrum.

items.en: Grammar: the genitive (whose?), the numbers one to ten, and quot? (how many?).
items.la: Grammatica: genitīvus (cuius?), numerī ab ūnō ad decem, et quot?

items.en: Grammar.
Whose is this pig? The pig is Bucca's. Whose is this wine? The wine is Bibulus's. It is no longer Bibulus's wine: Bibulus drinks it. "Buccae" and "Bibulī" are the genitive: whose a thing is.
items.la: Cuius est hic porcus? Porcus est Buccae. Cuius est hoc vīnum? Vīnum est Bibulī. Iam nōn est vīnum Bibulī: Bibulus id bibit. "Buccae" et "Bibulī" sunt genitīvus: cuius rēs est.

items.en: The genitive often stands after the thing: "Scaurus's house", "Bucca's nose", "the smell of the pigs". The smell of the pigs is strong. The smell of Bibulus is stronger.
items.la: Genitīvus saepe post rem stat: "domus Scaurī", "nāsus Buccae", "odor porcōrum". Odor porcōrum est fortis. Odor Bibulī est fortior.

items.en: Numbers: one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten. Quot? = how many?
items.la: Numerī: ūnus, duo, trēs, quattuor, quīnque, sex, septem, octō, novem, decem. Quot? = quam multī?

items.en: "How many pigs are in the pig pen?" — "Seven." "How many pigs are in the cookshop?" — "Eight, if you count Bibulus."
items.la: "Quot porcī sunt in harā?" — "Septem." "Quot porcī sunt in popīnā?" — "Octō, sī Bibulum numerās."

Reading one: The best fish sauce.
Bucca tastes the fish sauce and makes a plan.
items.la: Bucca garum gustat et cōnsilium capit.

items.en: The year is 125. Porcellus is now four years old. Porcellus is a small, fat boy.
items.la: Annus est centēsimus vīcēsimus quīntus. Porcellus nunc quattuor annōs habet. Porcellus est puer parvus et crassus.

items.en: Porcellus's nose is red. Porcellus's voice is loud, like Bucca's voice.
items.la: Nāsus Porcellī est rubicundus. Vōx Porcellī est magna, sīcut vōx Buccae.

items.en: Porcellus's feet are always dirty.
In the cookshop Bucca tastes the fish sauce. She makes a sad face.
items.la: In popīnā Bucca garum gustat. Faciem trīstem facit.

items.en: This fish sauce is bad.
All fish sauce is bad. Fish sauce is a dead fish in a pot.
items.la: Omne garum est malum. Garum est piscis mortuus in ollā.

items.en: No! There is good fish sauce. In the world there is the best fish sauce: the fish sauce of Scaurus.
items.la: Minimē! Est garum bonum. In mundō est garum optimum: garum Scaurī.

items.en: Whose?
Scaurus's! Umbricius Scaurus's! The fish sauce of Scaurus is the fish sauce of kings. The fish sauce of the gods!
items.la: Scaurī! Umbriciī Scaurī! Garum Scaurī est garum rēgum. Garum deōrum!

items.en: The fish sauce of the gods! Where is it?
In the town of Pompeii. In Campania. Near the sea.
items.la: In oppidō Pompēiīs. In Campāniā. Prope mare.

items.en: In Pompeii? Bucca... Pompeii...
What, Bibulus?
Nothing. Nothing. Why do you ask me? I am Bibulus. I know nothing.
items.la: Nihil. Nihil. Cūr mē rogās? Ego sum Bibulus. Ego nihil sciō.

items.en: Bucca counts her money: one coin, two coins, three coins... ten coins.
items.la: Bucca pecūniam numerat: ūnus nummus, duo nummī, trēs nummī… decem nummī.

items.en: Ten coins are Bucca's money. All of Bucca's money.
items.la: Decem nummī sunt pecūnia Buccae. Tōta pecūnia Buccae.

items.en: Tomorrow we go. Me, Porcellus and Bibulus. Bibulus carries the sack.
items.la: Crās īmus. Ego, Porcellus et Bibulus. Bibulus saccum portat.

items.en: Why me?
Because you always sit. The sack always sits too. You are friends.
items.la: Quia tū semper sedēs. Saccus quoque semper sedet. Amīcī estis.

items.en: Excursus: Mount Vesuvius. True!
What happened at Pompeii in the year 79?
items.la: Quid Pompēiīs accidit annō septuāgēsimō nōnō?

items.en: This is true. Near Pompeii there is a mountain: Vesuvius. In the year 79 Mount Vesuvius burns.
items.la: Hoc est vērum. Prope Pompēiōs est mōns: Vesuvius. Annō septuāgēsimō nōnō mōns Vesuvius ārdet.

items.en: Fire and ash and stones fall from the sky. The towns of Pompeii and Herculaneum lie under the ash.
items.la: Ignis et cinis et saxa dē caelō cadunt. Oppida Pompēiī et Herculāneum sub cinere iacent.

items.en: Many people die. Among them is a learned man, Pliny the Elder, who wants to see the burning mountain closer.
items.la: Multī hominēs moriuntur. Inter eōs est vir doctus, Plīnius Maior, quī montem ārdentem propius vidēre vult.

items.en: This is a bad plan.
In the year 125 Pompeii has already lain under the ash for forty-six years. People know the place.
items.la: Annō centēsimō vīcēsimō quīntō Pompēiī iam quadrāgintā sex annōs sub cinere iacent. Hominēs locum sciunt.

items.en: Some dig and look for precious things: gold, silver, statues. Afterwards people forget the place.
items.la: Nōnnūllī fodiunt et rēs pretiōsās quaerunt: aurum, argentum, statuās. Posteā hominēs locum oblīvīscuntur.

items.en: In the year 1748 people start to dig again. Today you can visit Pompeii: houses, streets, shops and walls full of writing.
items.la: Annō mīllēsimō septingentēsimō quadrāgēsimō octāvō hominēs iterum fodere incipiunt. Hodiē Pompēiōs vīsere potes: domūs, viās, tabernās et mūrōs plēnōs litterārum.

items.en: And the fish sauce? This too is true: Aulus Umbricius Scaurus makes and sells fish sauce in Pompeii.
items.la: Et garum? Etiam hoc est vērum: Aulus Umbricius Scaurus garum Pompēiīs facit et vēndit.

items.en: In Scaurus's house there are pictures of jars, and on the jars it is written: "The best fish sauce of Scaurus".
items.la: In domō Scaurī sunt imāginēs urceōrum, et in urceīs scrīptum est: "Garum optimum Scaurī".

items.en: Scaurus is the king of fish sauce. The king of rotten fish.
items.la: Scaurus est rēx garī. Rēx piscium putridōrum.

items.en: Reading two: Pompeii.
The trip to Pompeii. Where is the town? And who is the man in the ditch?
items.la: Iter ad Pompēiōs. Ubi est oppidum? Et quis est vir in fossā?

items.en: After three days Bucca, Porcellus and Bibulus stand near Pompeii. In front of them there is no town.
items.la: Post trēs diēs Bucca, Porcellus et Bibulus prope Pompēiōs stant. Ante eōs nōn est oppidum.

items.en: In front of them is a hill of ash. The hill is big, grey, silent. There are grass and two goats there.
items.la: Ante eōs est collis cineris. Collis est magnus, griseus, tacitus. Ibi sunt herbae et caprae duae.

items.en: Where is the town?
Look, the town.
This is not a town. This is ash.
items.la: Hoc nōn est oppidum. Hoc est cinis.

items.en: In the year 79 there was a town. Now it is ash. I want to tell you this, Bucca. But you talk, talk, talk.
items.la: Annō septuāgēsimō nōnō erat oppidum. Nunc est cinis. Hoc tibi dīcere volō, Bucca. Sed tū loqueris, loqueris, loqueris.

items.en: Where is the fish sauce of the gods?
Under the ash, little one. With Scaurus.
Suddenly a man comes out of a ditch. The man is small and thin. The man's tunic is dirty.
items.la: Subitō ex fossā venit vir. Vir est parvus et macer. Tunica virī est sordida.

items.en: The man's eyes are quick. The man's name is Furius.
items.la: Oculī virī sunt celerēs. Nōmen virī est Fūrius.

items.en: Hello, friends! Are you looking for fish sauce? Scaurus's fish sauce?
items.la: Salvēte, amīcī! Garum quaeritis? Garum Scaurī?

items.en: Yes! How do you know?
Everybody is looking for Scaurus's fish sauce. I have Scaurus's fish sauce. Real fish sauce! Forty-six years under the ash.
items.la: Omnēs garum Scaurī quaerunt. Ego garum Scaurī habeō. Vērum garum! Quadrāgintā sex annōs sub cinere.

items.en: Old fish sauce is good fish sauce!
Furius shows a jar. On the jar it is written: "GARUM OF SCAURUS". The letters are new.
items.la: Fūrius urceum ostendit. In urceō est scrīptum: "GARVM SCAVRI". Litterae sunt novae.

items.en: The ink is wet.
The ink is wet.
It is... it is the dampness of the ash. The ash is damp.
items.la: Est… est ūmor cineris. Cinis est ūmidus.

items.en: How much does it cost?
Ten coins.
Ten! I have ten coins!
What a wonder! That is the price. The gods want it.
items.la: Quid mīrum! Hoc est pretium. Deī volunt.

items.en: The gods want it, or Furius wants it?
The gods and Furius are friends.
Furius leads them into the ditch. Under the earth is an old street. There are walls, shops, doors.
items.la: Fūrius eōs in fossam dūcit. Sub terrā est via antīqua. Sunt mūrī, tabernae, iānuae.

items.en: On the walls there are many letters: names, words, pictures.
items.la: In mūrīs sunt multae litterae: nōmina, verba, imāginēs.

items.en: What is this? And this? And this?
items.la: Quid est hoc? Et hoc? Et hoc?

items.en: These are verses. The people of Pompeii write on the walls. Everyone writes. Boys, women, neighbours, drunks.
items.la: Hī sunt versūs. Pompēiānī in mūrīs scrībunt. Omnēs scrībunt. Puerī, fēminae, vīcīnī, ēbriī.

items.en: What do the walls say?
Listen.
A real Latin text: Pompēiī, CIL IV 4957, 3146, 1904.
The walls of Pompeii speak. And they do not speak nicely.
items.la: Mūrī Pompēiānī loquuntur. Et nōn bene loquuntur.

items.en: Furius reads the verses on the walls and explains them. The first verse is on the wall of an inn: guests wet the bed, because there is no chamber pot in the bedroom.
items.la: Fūrius versūs in mūrīs legit et explicat. Prīmus versus est in mūrō dēversōriī: hospitēs in lectō mingunt, quia in cubiculō nūlla matella est.

items.en: A chamber pot is a small pot: at night you pee in it. The guests admit the blame, but they give a reason.
items.la: Matella est vās parvum: in eō nocte mingis. Hospitēs culpam fatentur, sed causam dant.

items.en: The second verse is short: "Secundus shits here." The third verse is about the wall itself: the wall is tired, because everybody writes on it.
items.la: Secundus versus est brevis: "Secundus hīc cacat." Tertius versus est dē mūrō ipsō: mūrus est fessus, quia omnēs in eō scrībunt.

items.en: The real text.
We wet the bed. I admit it, we did wrong, host.
items.la: Miximus in lecto. Fateor, peccavimus, hospes.

items.en: If you say: why? There was no chamber pot.
items.la: Si dices: quare? Nulla matella fuit.

items.en: Secundus shits here.
I wonder, o wall, that you have not fallen down in ruins,
items.la: Admiror, o paries, te non cecidisse ruinis,

items.en: you who hold up the boring stuff of so many writers.

Three real Pompeii wall writings, Corpus Inscriptionum Latinarum (CIL) volume IV. (1) CIL IV 4957, in an inn: "We pissed in the bed. I admit it, host, we did wrong. If you ask why: there was no chamber pot." It is a neat elegiac couplet. Poetry, about piss. (2) CIL IV 3146: "Secundus shits here." Rome's oldest status update. (3) CIL IV 1904 and copies: "I am amazed, O wall, that you have not fallen down in ruins, you who carry the boring scribbles of so many writers." Grammar to spot: genitive plural "scriptorum" (of writers), "tot" = so many, "te non cecidisse" = that you have not fallen (accusative + infinitive, coming later in this book).
Reading three: Furius's fish sauce.
Bucca buys the fish sauce. What is in the jar?
items.la: Bucca garum emit. Quid est in urceō?

items.en: "Secundus shits here"? Who is Secundus?
The astrologer! Secundus the astrologer!
Perhaps. Astrologers shit everywhere.
Porcellus finds a piece of charcoal on the ground. Porcellus wants to write on the wall. But Porcellus does not know his letters.
items.la: Porcellus carbōnem in terrā invenit. Porcellus in mūrō scrībere vult. Sed Porcellus litterās nōn scit.

items.en: Porcellus draws a pig. Porcellus's pig has four feet and a tail and a big nose.
items.la: Porcellus porcum pingit. Porcus Porcellī quattuor pedēs habet et caudam et nāsum magnum.

items.en: Under the pig Porcellus draws... something. Nobody knows what. Even today nobody knows.
items.la: Sub porcō Porcellus pingit… aliquid. Nēmō scit quid. Etiam hodiē nēmō scit.

items.en: Bucca gives the ten coins to Furius. Furius gives the jar to Bucca. Furius laughs. Furius runs.
items.la: Bucca decem nummōs Fūriō dat. Fūrius urceum Buccae dat. Fūrius cachinnat. Fūrius currit.

items.en: Furius is gone.
A kind man.
A quick man.
In the street Bucca opens the jar. Bucca tastes the fish sauce. Bucca's face changes.
items.la: In viā Bucca urceum aperit. Bucca garum gustat. Faciēs Buccae mūtātur.

items.en: First it is red. Then it is white. Then it is green.
items.la: Prīmum est rubra. Deinde est alba. Deinde est viridis.

items.en: Is it the fish sauce of the gods?
It is... sea water. And salt. And... one fish. One small fish. And the fish is alive!
items.la: Est… aqua marīna. Et sāl. Et… piscis ūnus. Ūnus parvus piscis. Et piscis vīvit!

items.en: The fish jumps out of the jar. Porcellus catches the fish. Porcellus kisses the fish.
items.la: Piscis ex urceō salit. Porcellus piscem capit. Porcellus piscem ōsculātur.

items.en: My friend!
Bucca, I want to tell you: Pompeii...
BE QUIET, BIBULUS!
They go back home. Bucca has no coins. Bibulus carries the sack: in the sack is Furius's jar.
items.la: Domum redeunt. Bucca nūllōs nummōs habet. Bibulus saccum portat: in saccō est urceus Fūriī.

items.en: Porcellus carries the fish. The fish is happy. The fish is the only one who is happy.
items.la: Porcellus piscem portat. Piscis est laetus. Piscis est sōlus laetus.

items.en: In front of the door of the big house sits little Marcus. Marcus too is four years old.
items.la: Ante iānuam domūs magnae sedet Marcus parvus. Marcus quoque quattuor annōs habet.

items.en: Marcus is reading a book. Marcus already reads, at four years old.
items.la: Marcus librum legit. Marcus iam legit, quattuor annōs nātus.

items.en: What are you doing?
I am reading. The book is about philosophy.
I have a fish.
Whose is the fish?
Mine! The fish of Porcellus!
The fish is not yours. The fish belongs to the sea. The fish is its own master.
items.la: Piscis nōn est tuus. Piscis est maris. Piscis est suī iūris.

items.en: Porcellus thinks for a long time. Porcellus takes Marcus's book and eats it.
items.la: Porcellus diū cōgitat. Porcellus librum Marcī capit et edit.

items.en: In the margin: Brother Unknown.
Brother Unknown on walls and on margins.
items.la: Frāter Ignōtus dē mūrīs et dē marginibus.

items.en: I, Brother Unknown, have read this chapter. The walls of Pompeii are disgusting. But we monks also write in books, in the margins.
items.la: Ego, Frāter Ignōtus, hoc capitulum lēgī. Mūrī Pompēiānī sunt foedī. Sed et nōs, mōnachī, in librīs scrībimus, in marginibus.

items.en: Brother Walter writes: "Oh, my hand." Brother Hugh writes: "This ink is bad." I write nothing.
items.la: Frāter Gualterus scrībit: "Ō, manus mea." Frāter Hugō scrībit: "Hoc ātrāmentum est malum." Ego nihil scrībō.

items.en: I am a good monk.
An old saying of scribes, at the end of a book: "Here ends the whole thing; for Christ's sake, give me a drink." That is: the book is finished; for Christ's sake, give me something to drink.
items.la: Vetus verbum scrīptōrum, in fīne librī: "Explicit hoc tōtum; prō Chrīstō dā mihi pōtum." Id est: liber est fīnītus; prō Chrīstō, dā mihi aliquid ad bibendum.

items.en: I love this saying. Bibulus loves this saying too.
items.la: Hoc verbum amō. Bibulus quoque hoc verbum amat.

items.en: Epilogue: what happened?

Bucca wanted Scaurus's fish sauce. So she went to Pompeii with Porcellus and Bibulus. But they did not find the town: only ash. Fūrius came out of a ditch and sold a jar. Under the ground they read filthy verses on the walls.
items.la: Bucca garum Scaurī voluit. Itaque cum Porcellō et Bibulō Pompēiōs iit. Sed oppidum nōn invēnērunt: tantum cinerem. Fūrius ex fossā vēnit et urceum vēndidit. Sub terrā versūs foedōs in mūrīs lēgērunt.

items.en: Porcellus painted a pig on the wall. Bucca paid ten coins, and in the jar there were water, salt and a live fish. In Rome, in front of the big house, Porcellus ate Marcus's book.
items.la: Porcellus porcum in mūrō pīnxit. Bucca decem nummōs dedit, et in urceō erant aqua, sāl et piscis vīvus. Rōmae, ante domum magnam, Porcellus librum Marcī ēdit.

items.en: What next?
Porcellus now has a fish for a friend and a book in his belly. Soon Porcellus will see a beautiful horse, and the emperor himself. And the emperor will give him a new name. Not a good name.
items.la: Porcellus nunc piscem amīcum habet et librum in ventre. Mox Porcellus equum pulchrum vidēbit, et imperātōrem ipsum. Et imperātor eī nōmen novum dabit. Nōmen nōn bonum.

items.en: Vir Rōmānus. Chapter three: Truest and Falsest.
Prologue: what will happen?

It is the year 127. Porcellus is six and he is a naughty boy. Today the emperor Hadrian comes to the Caelian hill and gives Marcus a horse. Porcellus wants a horse too. But Porcellus does not have a horse. Porcellus has a pig.
items.la: Annus est centēsimus vīcēsimus septimus. Porcellus sex annōs habet et est puer improbus. Hodiē Hadriānus imperātor in montem Caelium venit et Marcō equum dat. Porcellus quoque equum vult. Sed Porcellus equum nōn habet. Porcellus porcum habet.

items.en: Grammar: the accusative (whom? what?), verbs (-at, -et, -it; -ant, -ent, -unt), the imperative (Come!) and the vocative (Porcellus!).
items.la: Grammatica: accūsātīvus (quem? quid?), verba (-at, -et, -it; -ant, -ent, -unt), imperātīvus (Venī!) et vocātīvus (Porcelle!).

items.en: Grammar.

Porcellus eats a cabbage. What does Porcellus eat? A cabbage. "Caulem" is the accusative: the thing that someone sees, takes, eats, hits. Bucca hits Porcellus. Whom does Bucca hit? Porcellus. Porcellus is the accusative. Porcellus is often the accusative.
items.la: Porcellus caulem edit. Quid edit Porcellus? Caulem. "Caulem" est accūsātīvus: rēs quam aliquis videt, capit, edit, pulsat. Bucca Porcellum pulsat. Quem pulsat Bucca? Porcellum. Porcellus est accūsātīvus. Porcellus est saepe accūsātīvus.

items.en: "Ōvum" does not change. The neuter is lazy: nominative and accusative are the same. Like Bibulus: sitting or lying, he is the same.
items.la: Ōvum nōn mūtātur. Neutrum est pigrum: nōminātīvus et accūsātīvus sunt idem. Sīcut Bibulus: sedēns et iacēns, idem est.

items.en: Verbs. One person does it: loves, sees, reads, hears. Many do it: they love, see, read, hear. Porcellus runs; the pigs run; Bibulus does not run.
items.la: Verba. Ūnus agit: amat, videt, legit, audit. Multī agunt: amant, vident, legunt, audiunt. Porcellus currit; porcī currunt; Bibulus nōn currit.

items.en: The imperative = giving an order. To one: Walk! Be quiet! Read! Listen! To many: Walk! Be quiet! Read! Listen! Every day Bucca says: "Come! Be quiet! Put that cabbage down!"
items.la: Imperātīvus = iubēre. Ūnī: Ambulā! Tacē! Lege! Audī! Multīs: Ambulāte! Tacēte! Legite! Audīte! Bucca cotīdiē dīcit: "Venī! Tacē! Dēpōne illum caulem!"

items.en: The vocative = calling someone. "Porcellus" → "Porcellus!" Bucca shouts: "Porcellus!" Porcellus does not come. This is a useless vocative.
items.la: Vocātīvus = vocāre. "Porcellus" → "Porcelle!" "Marcus" → "Marce!" "Tertius" → "Tertī!" Bucca clāmat: "Porcelle!" Porcellus nōn venit. Hic est vocātīvus inūtilis.

Reading one: A big day.
A big day. Porcellus grabs sausages; Marcus reads.
items.la: Diēs magnus. Porcellus botulōs rapit; Marcus legit.

items.en: The year is 127. Porcellus is six years old. Porcellus is not a good boy.
items.la: Annus est centēsimus vīcēsimus septimus. Porcellus sex annōs habet. Porcellus nōn est puer bonus.

items.en: Porcellus is a naughty boy.
Today is a big day on the Caelian hill. The emperor Hadrian is coming back to Rome.
items.la: Hodiē est diēs magnus in monte Caeliō. Imperātor Hadriānus Rōmam redit.

items.en: Hadrian visits Marcus. The emperor loves the boy Marcus. Everybody knows this.
items.la: Hadriānus Marcum vīsitat. Imperātor puerum Marcum amat. Omnēs hoc sciunt.

items.en: Today the emperor gives Marcus a gift: a horse.
items.la: Hodiē imperātor Marcō dōnum dat: equum.

items.en: Slaves clean the street. The slaves take away the pigs' dung. The pigs make new dung.
items.la: Servī viam pūrgant. Servī stercus porcōrum tollunt. Porcī novum stercus faciunt.

items.en: The slaves are angry. The pigs are happy. That is life.
items.la: Servī īrātī sunt. Porcī laetī sunt. Haec est vīta.

items.en: Bucca stands in front of the cookshop. Bucca is selling sausages. The sausages are hot and fat and strange.
items.la: Bucca ante popīnam stat. Bucca botulōs vēndit. Botulī sunt calidī et pinguēs et mīrī.

items.en: What is in the sausages? Nobody knows. Bucca knows. Bucca does not say.
items.la: Quid est in botulīs? Nēmō scit. Bucca scit. Bucca nōn dīcit.

items.en: Sausages! Hot sausages! One as! Buy sausages!
items.la: Botulī! Botulī calidī! Ūnus as! Emite botulōs!

items.en: What is in the sausages?
Meat.
Whose meat?
Meat... of an animal.
Of what animal?
Of a dead animal. Are you buying or not?
items.la: Animālis mortuī. Emis an nōn emis?

items.en: Porcellus grabs a sausage. Porcellus runs. Bucca shouts.
items.la: Porcellus botulum capit. Porcellus currit. Bucca clāmat.

items.en: Porcellus! Come here! Put the sausage down!
Porcellus does not come. Porcellus eats the sausage. Then Porcellus grabs a cabbage and hits a slave.
items.la: Porcellus nōn venit. Porcellus botulum edit. Deinde Porcellus caulem capit et servum pulsat.

items.en: The slave falls into the dung. A dog barks. Porcellus hits the dog. The dog bites Porcellus.
items.la: Servus cadit in stercus. Canis lātrat. Porcellus canem pulsat. Canis Porcellum mordet.

items.en: Porcellus cries.
Bucca! The dog is biting me!
The dog does well.
On the steps of the big house sits Marcus. Marcus too is six years old. Marcus is reading a book.
items.la: In gradibus domūs magnae sedet Marcus. Marcus quoque sex annōs habet. Marcus librum legit.

items.en: An old woman is carrying a heavy sack. Marcus gets up and helps the woman. Then Marcus sits down again and reads.
items.la: Fēmina vetus saccum gravem portat. Marcus surgit et fēminam adiuvat. Deinde Marcus iterum sedet et legit.

items.en: Why are you always good?
Because I want to be a philosopher.
What is a philosopher?
A man who thinks. A man who looks for the truth.
items.la: Vir quī cōgitat. Vir quī vēritātem quaerit.

items.en: I think too. I always think.
What do you think about?
About sausages.
Hmm. It is a beginning.
Excursus: Roman names. True!
Why do Romans have three names? And why is one name "Porcius"?
items.la: Cūr Rōmānī tria nōmina habent? Et cūr ūnum nōmen est "Porcius"?

items.en: This is true. A Roman man often has three names. The first is the praenomen, the first name: Marcus, Gaius, Lucius, Quintus.
items.la: Hoc est vērum. Vir Rōmānus saepe tria nōmina habet. Prīmum est praenōmen: Marcus, Gāius, Lūcius, Quīntus.

items.en: The second is the nomen: the family name, like Julius, Cornelius, Annius. The third is the cognomen: often about the body or about an animal.
items.la: Secundum est nōmen: nōmen familiae, ut Iūlius, Cornēlius, Annius. Tertium est cognōmen: saepe dē corpore aut dē animālī.

items.en: Cicero = cicer, that is a small bean: Cicero's grandfather perhaps has a wart on his nose, like a chickpea.
items.la: Cicerō = cicer, id est legūmen parvum: avus Cicerōnis fortasse in nāsō verrūcam habet, similem ciceris.

items.en: Naso = a man with a big nose: the poet Ovid is "Publius Ovidius Naso". Scrofa = a sow.
items.la: Nāsō = vir cum nāsō magnō: poēta Ovidius est "Pūblius Ovidius Nāsō". Scrōfa = porca.

items.en: And that strict Cato? Marcus Porcius Cato. The name "Porcius" comes from a pig.
items.la: Et Catō ille sevērus? Marcus Porcius Catō. Nōmen "Porcius" venit ā porcō.

items.en: So Porcellus is in good company.
items.la: Porcellus igitur est in bonā societāte.

items.en: Our Marcus has many names. The Historia Augusta says: first Marcus is called Catilius Severus; then Annius Verus; later Aurelius.
items.la: Marcus noster multa nōmina habet. Historia Augusta dīcit: prīmum Marcus vocātur Catilius Sevērus; deinde Annius Vērus; posteā Aurēlius.

items.en: Marcus changes names, the way other men change tunics.
items.la: Marcus nōmina mūtat, sīcut aliī virī tunicās.

items.en: Reading two: The horse and the pig.
Hadrian comes. Marcus gets a horse. Porcellus jumps on a pig.
items.la: Hadriānus venit. Marcus equum accipit. Porcellus in porcum salit.

items.en: Trumpets sound. Soldiers come. After the soldiers comes a tall man with a beard: Hadrian.
items.la: Tubae canunt. Mīlitēs veniunt. Post mīlitēs venit vir altus cum barbā: Hadriānus.

items.en: Everyone kneels. Bibulus kneels too, because Bibulus is already lying down.
items.la: Omnēs genua flectunt. Bibulus quoque genua flectit, quia Bibulus iam iacet.

items.en: A slave leads a small horse. The horse is white and beautiful. Marcus walks to the emperor.
items.la: Servus equum parvum dūcit. Equus est albus et pulcher. Marcus ad imperātōrem ambulat.

items.en: Hello, Marcus! This horse is yours. You are now a Roman knight.
items.la: Salvē, Marce! Hic equus est tuus. Tū nunc es eques Rōmānus.

items.en: I thank you, emperor. I will look after the horse. I will not ride without a reason.
items.la: Grātiās tibi agō, imperātor. Equum cūrābō. Nōn equitābō sine causā.

items.en: Ha! Listen! A boy of six! "I will not ride without a reason!" You are not Verus, Marcus, not just True. You are Verissimus, Truest of all!
items.la: Ha! Audīte! Puer sex annōrum! "Nōn equitābō sine causā!" Tū nōn es Vērus, Marce. Tū es Vērissimus!

items.en: Everyone laughs. Everyone claps. Porcellus does not clap. Porcellus looks at the horse.
items.la: Omnēs cachinnant. Omnēs plaudunt. Porcellus nōn plaudit. Porcellus spectat equum.

items.en: Porcellus looks at Marcus. Porcellus looks at a big pig, which is lying near the cookshop.
items.la: Porcellus spectat Marcum. Porcellus spectat porcum magnum, quī prope popīnam iacet.

items.en: The pig is called Caesar.
Caesar! Come here!
Caesar does not come. Porcellus jumps onto Caesar. Caesar gets up. Caesar runs.
items.la: Caesar nōn venit. Porcellus in Caesarem salit. Caesar surgit. Caesar currit.

items.en: Caesar does not run to the pig pen. Caesar runs to the emperor.
items.la: Caesar nōn ad haram currit. Caesar ad imperātōrem currit.

items.en: What is this?
A pig.
And what is on the pig?
Another pig.
Caesar runs among the soldiers. The soldiers fall. Caesar snatches a laurel crown from a slave's head and eats it.
items.la: Caesar inter mīlitēs currit. Mīlitēs cadunt. Caesar corōnam lauream dē capite servī rapit et edit.

items.en: At last Caesar stops in front of Hadrian. Porcellus sits on Caesar, dirty and happy.
items.la: Tandem Caesar ante Hadriānum cōnsistit. Porcellus in Caesare sedet, sordidus et laetus.

items.en: Who are you?
I am the emperor!
Really? And I, what am I?
You are... bearded.
Silence. The soldiers hold their swords. Bucca closes her eyes. Bibulus sees nothing, because he is asleep.
items.la: Silentium. Mīlitēs gladiōs tenent. Bucca oculōs claudit. Bibulus nihil videt, quia dormit.

items.en: Who is this boy?
This is Porcellus, my lord. The astrologers say: this is the future emperor.
items.la: Hic est Porcellus, domine. Astrologī dīcunt: hic est imperātor futūrus.

items.en: Astrologers! Ha! I love astrologers. Astrologers are always wrong. Marcus, come here! Look, Romans!
items.la: Astrologī! Ha! Ego astrologōs amō. Astrologī semper errant. Marce, venī! Spectāte, Rōmānī!

items.en: This one, Marcus, is Verissimus, the Truest. That one, Porcellus, is... Falsissimus, the Falsest!
items.la: Hic, Marcus, est Vērissimus. Ille, Porcellus, est… Falsissimus!

items.en: Everyone laughs. Even the soldiers laugh. Caesar the pig farts. Everyone laughs more.
items.la: Omnēs cachinnant. Etiam mīlitēs cachinnant. Caesar porcus pēdit. Omnēs cachinnant magis.

items.en: Falsissimus! Do you hear, Bibulus? The emperor names my son! Falsissimus! A great name!
items.la: Falsissimus! Audīsne, Bibule? Imperātor fīlium meum nōminat! Falsissimus! Nōmen magnum!

items.en: Bucca... "false"...
Be quiet, Bibulus! It is a great name!
A real Latin text: Historia Augusta, Vīta Marcī 4.1–3.
items.la: Textus vērus: Historia Augusta, Vīta Marcī.

items.en: A real book: what does Hadrian really give Marcus?
items.la: Liber vērus: quid Hadriānus Marcō vērē dat?

items.en: The Historia Augusta tells about Marcus. Hadrian loves the boy Marcus and calls him "Verissimus".
items.la: Historia Augusta dē Marcō nārrat. Hadriānus puerum Marcum amat et eum "Vērissimum" vocat.

items.en: Marcus is six years old: Hadrian gives him the honour of a horse. Marcus is seven years old: Marcus becomes a priest of the Salii.
items.la: Marcus sex annōs habet: Hadriānus eī honōrem equī dat. Marcus septem annōs habet: Marcus fit sacerdōs Saliōrum.

items.en: The Salii are priests who dance. All the priests throw crowns. The crowns fall, some in one place, some in another.
items.la: Saliī sunt sacerdōtēs quī saltant. Omnēs sacerdōtēs corōnās iaciunt. Corōnae aliae aliīs locīs cadunt.

items.en: Marcus's crown falls onto the head of the god Mars, as if placed there by hand. This is a sign: Marcus will be emperor.
items.la: Corōna Marcī in capite deī Martis cadit, quasi manū positā. Hoc est signum: Marcus erit imperātor.

items.en: The real text.
He was brought up in Hadrian's lap, who used to call him Verissimus,
items.la: Educatus est in Hadriani gremio, qui illum Verissimum nominabat

items.en: and who gave him the honour of a public horse at six years old,
items.la: et qui ei honorem equi publici sexenni detulit,

items.en: and in the eighth year of his age enrolled him in the college of the Salii.
items.la: octavo aetatis anno in saliorum collegium rettulit.

items.en: In the priesthood of the Salii he received an omen of empire: when all were throwing crowns onto the sacred couch, as is the custom,
items.la: In saliatu omen accepit imperii: coronas omnibus in pulvinar ex more iacientibus

items.en: the others stuck in different places, but his was fitted onto the head of Mars, as if by hand.
items.la: aliae aliis locis haeserunt, huius velut manu capiti Martis aptata est.

items.en: Real text, Historia Augusta, Life of Marcus 4.1–3. Hadrian really called the boy "Verissimus" (the truest, a pun on his family name Verus), and gave him the honour of the "public horse" (the badge of a Roman knight) at six. In his eighth year (aged seven) Marcus joined the Salii, the leaping priests of Mars, who danced through Rome in armour. When all the priests threw their crowns onto the god's couch, Marcus's crown landed on the head of Mars, "as if put there by hand": an omen of empire. Grammar to spot: accusative "illum", "honorem", "coronas"; "sexenni" = to the six-year-old; "omnibus ... iacientibus" = while all were throwing (an ablative absolute, Part II).
Reading three: The frog and the ox.
Porcellus is sad. Marcus tells a story.
items.la: Porcellus trīstis est. Marcus fābulam nārrat.

items.en: In the evening Porcellus and Marcus sit on the steps. Caesar the pig sleeps near them.
items.la: Vesperī Porcellus et Marcus in gradibus sedent. Caesar porcus prope eōs dormit.

items.en: Porcellus is sad.
You are Verissimus. I am Falsissimus. Everyone laughs.
items.la: Tū es Vērissimus. Ego sum Falsissimus. Omnēs cachinnant.

items.en: Everyone laughs because you sit on a pig.
items.la: Omnēs cachinnant, quia tū in porcō sedēs.

items.en: I want to be big. Big like you. Big like the emperor.
items.la: Ego volō esse magnus. Magnus sīcut tū. Magnus sīcut imperātor.

items.en: Listen to a story. Phaedrus tells it.
A real Latin text: Phaedrus, Fābulae 1.24.
A fable by Phaedrus: a small frog, a big ox.
items.la: Fābula Phaedrī: rāna parva, bōs magnus.

items.en: Marcus tells the story. In a meadow a frog sees an ox. The ox is big. The frog is small.
items.la: Marcus fābulam nārrat. In prātō rāna bovem videt. Bōs est magnus. Rāna est parva.

items.en: The frog is jealous. The frog puffs up her skin and asks her children: "Am I wider than the ox?" The children say: "No." The frog puffs herself up again.
items.la: Rāna invidet. Rāna pellem īnflat et fīliōs rogat: "Sumne lātior quam bōs?" Fīliī dīcunt: "Minimē." Rāna iterum sē īnflat.

items.en: "Who is bigger now?" The children say: "The ox." At last the frog puffs herself up too much.
items.la: "Quis nunc est maior?" Fīliī dīcunt: "Bōs." Tandem rāna sē nimis īnflat.

items.en: The frog bursts. She lies dead.
The real text.
The poor man, while he wants to copy the powerful, dies.
items.la: Inops, potentem dum vult imitari, perit.

items.en: Once in a meadow a frog caught sight of an ox,
items.la: In prato quondam rana conspexit bovem,

items.en: and, touched by envy of such great size,
she puffed up her wrinkled skin. Then she asked her children
items.la: rugosam inflavit pellem. Tum natos suos

items.en: whether she was wider than the ox.
They said no. Again she stretched her skin
with greater effort, and asked in the same way
items.la: maiore nisu, et simili quaesivit modo,

items.en: who was bigger. They said: "The ox."
At last, angry, while she wants to puff herself up
more strongly, she lay with her body burst.

Phaedrus, Fables 1.24, "The frog that burst and the ox", in verse (iambic senarii), about 40 AD. Phaedrus was a freed slave of the emperor Augustus who put Aesop's Greek fables into Latin. The first line is the moral: "The poor man dies while he tries to copy the powerful." Watch the accusatives: "bovem", "pellem", "cutem". "Rupto ... corpore" = with her body burst (ablative). Porcellus will take the wrong lesson from this.
Reading four: Porcellus puffed up.
Porcellus understands the story. Badly.
Do you understand, Porcellus?
I understand! The frog is small because she does not eat enough!
items.la: Intellegō! Rāna est parva, quia nōn satis edit!

items.en: No! That is not...
But Porcellus is already running. Porcellus runs into the cookshop. Porcellus grabs sausages: one, two, three... ten... twenty.
items.la: Sed Porcellus iam currit. Porcellus in popīnam currit. Porcellus botulōs capit: ūnum, duōs, trēs… decem… vīgintī.

items.en: Porcellus eats the sausages. Porcellus puffs out his cheeks. Porcellus puffs out his belly.
items.la: Porcellus botulōs edit. Porcellus genās īnflat. Porcellus ventrem īnflat.

items.en: Marcus! Am I bigger than you?
You are not bigger. You are rounder.
Porcellus eats another sausage. And another. Porcellus's belly is huge.
items.la: Porcellus alterum botulum edit. Et alterum. Venter Porcellī est ingēns.

items.en: Porcellus's belly is like the sky: round and full of thunder.
items.la: Venter Porcellī est sīcut caelum: rotundus et plēnus tonitrūs.

items.en: And then... Porcellus does not burst. Porcellus farts. The sound is huge. Dogs bark on the whole Caelian hill.
items.la: Et tum… Porcellus nōn rumpitur. Porcellus pēdit. Sonus est ingēns. Canēs in tōtō monte Caeliō lātrant.

items.en: The lamps in the big house shake. Caesar the pig wakes up and runs away. Bibulus wakes up and says: "Has summer come?"
items.la: Lucernae in domō magnā tremunt. Caesar porcus ēvigilat et fugit. Bibulus ēvigilat et dīcit: "Vēnit aestās?"

items.en: PORCELLUS!
Phaedrus writes nothing about this.
I am now writing a new story. "Porcellus and the sausages." A good ending.
items.la: Ego nunc scrībō fābulam novam. "Porcellus et botulī." Fīnis bonus.

items.en: In the margin: Brother Unknown.
Brother Unknown on frogs and on the abbot.
items.la: Frāter Ignōtus dē rānīs et dē abbāte.

items.en: I, Brother Unknown, love Phaedrus. Aesop, Phaedrus, animal stories: these are good for novices.
items.la: Ego, Frāter Ignōtus, Phaedrum amō. Aesōpus, Phaedrus, fābulae animālium: haec sunt bona prō novīciīs.

items.en: The proud frog bursts. Our abbot too is proud. Our abbot too often puffs himself up.
items.la: Rāna superba rumpitur. Abbās noster quoque superbus est. Abbās noster quoque saepe īnflātur.

items.en: I say no more.
But this Porcellus is disgusting. Why do I write this? Because the abbot orders it. And because, I admit it, I laugh.
items.la: Sed hic Porcellus est foedus. Cūr hoc scrībō? Quia abbās iubet. Et quia, fateor, cachinnō.

items.en: May God forgive me.
An old saying of scribes: "When the book is finished, the scribe dances with a happy foot." When the book is finished, the scribe dances on a happy foot.
items.la: Vetus verbum scrīptōrum: "Librō complētō saltat scrīptor pede laetō." Ubi liber est complētus, scrīptor laetō pede saltat.

items.en: The book is not finished. My feet do not dance.
items.la: Liber nōn est complētus. Pedēs meī nōn saltant.

items.en: Epilogue: what happened?

Hadrian came back to Rome and gave Marcus a horse. Porcellus grabbed Bucca's sausages and hit a slave with a cabbage. Then he jumped onto Caesar the pig and ran among the soldiers. Hadrian laughed. He called Marcus "Truest" and Porcellus "Falsest".
items.la: Hadriānus Rōmam rediit et Marcō equum dedit. Porcellus botulōs Buccae rapuit et servum caule pulsāvit. Deinde in porcum Caesarem saluit et inter mīlitēs cucurrit. Hadriānus rīsit. Marcum "Vērissimum", Porcellum "Falsissimum" vocāvit.

items.en: Bucca loved the name, but she did not understand it. In the evening Marcus told the fable of the frog. Porcellus ate twenty sausages. He did not burst. He farted.
items.la: Bucca nōmen amāvit, sed nōn intellēxit. Vesperī Marcus fābulam dē rānā nārrāvit. Porcellus vīgintī botulōs ēdit. Nōn ruptus est. Pepēdit.

items.en: What next?
Falsest now has a name, but he has no money. Bucca wants to buy a slave, because Porcellus does no work. In the forum there is a fat trader and a Greek slave who speaks five languages. Really?
items.la: Falsissimus nunc nōmen habet, sed pecūniam nōn habet. Bucca servum emere vult, quia Porcellus nihil labōrat. In forō est mercātor crassus et servus Graecus quī quīnque linguās loquitur. Vērumne?

items.en: Vir Rōmānus. Chapter four: The useless slave.
Prologue: what will happen?

It is the year 128. Bucca works too hard and wants to buy a slave. In the forum a trader sells her a Greek slave, a philosopher, called Sabidius. Sabidius talks a lot and does nothing. Then Bibulus is ill, and a strange doctor comes.
items.la: Annus est centēsimus vīcēsimus octāvus. Bucca nimis labōrat et servum emere vult. In forō mercātor eī servum Graecum vēndit, philosophum, Sabidium nōmine. Sabidius multum loquitur et nihil facit. Deinde Bibulus aeger est, et venit medicus mīrus.

items.en: Grammar: the dative (to whom?), is ea id, numbers up to a thousand, and Roman money.
items.la: Grammatica: datīvus (cui?), is ea id, numerī ad mīlle, et pecūnia Rōmāna.

items.en: Grammar.

Bucca gives money to the trader. To whom does Bucca give money? To the trader. "Mercātōrī" is the dative: the one to whom something is given, said, shown. Bucca does not give wine to Bibulus. Bibulus gives wine to himself.
items.la: Bucca mercātōrī pecūniam dat. Cui dat Bucca pecūniam? Mercātōrī. "Mercātōrī" est datīvus: is cui aliquid datur, dīcitur, mōnstrātur. Bucca Bibulō vīnum nōn dat. Bibulus sibi vīnum dat.

items.en: Remember: "puellae" is genitive and dative. The girl is busy.
items.la: Mementō: "puellae" est genitīvus et datīvus. Puella est occupāta.

items.en: Is, ea, id = he, she, it. But also him, her, to him/her, his/her. "I see a slave. I buy him. I give him food. His name is Sabidius. I do not love him."
items.la: Is, ea, id: vir, fēmina, rēs. Sed etiam eum, eam, eī, eius. "Servum videō. Eum emō. Eī cibum dō. Nōmen eius est Sabidius. Eum nōn amō."

items.en: Numbers: ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty... a hundred, two hundred, three hundred... five hundred... a thousand. A thousand is a big number. A thousand sausages are a small dinner for Porcellus.
items.la: Numerī: decem, vīgintī, trīgintā, quadrāgintā, quīnquāgintā… centum, ducentī, trecentī… quīngentī… mīlle. Mīlle est numerus magnus. Mīlle botulī sunt cēna parva prō Porcellō.
