Reading one: In the forum.
Bucca, Porcellus and Bibulus go to the slave market.
items.la: Bucca, Porcellus et Bibulus ad mercātum servōrum eunt.

items.en: The year is 128. Porcellus is seven years old. Bucca's cookshop is full of people.
items.la: Annus est centēsimus vīcēsimus octāvus. Porcellus septem annōs habet. Popīna Buccae est plēna hominum.

items.en: Bucca works; Bucca cooks; Bucca shouts. Does Porcellus work? No. Porcellus eats.
items.la: Bucca labōrat; Bucca coquit; Bucca clāmat. Porcellus labōrat? Minimē. Porcellus edit.

items.en: Does Bibulus work? That is ridiculous.
Enough! I am buying a slave. The slave works; I sleep.
items.la: Satis! Servum emō. Servus labōrat; ego dormiō.

items.en: A slave costs a lot.
I have money. The astrologers gave me gold, and I am keeping it. I have been keeping it for six years.
items.la: Pecūniam habeō. Astrologī mihi aurum dedērunt, et ego id servō. Sex annōs id servō.

items.en: My gold!
Your gold? You have cost me six years. Sausages, cabbages, fish sauce. Your gold is my gold.
items.la: Tuum aurum? Tū mihi sex annōs cōnstās. Botulōs, caulēs, garum. Tuum aurum est meum aurum.

items.en: In the forum, near the temple of Castor, there is a slave market. The slaves stand on a platform.
items.la: In forō, prope templum Castoris, est mercātus servōrum. Servī in tabulā stant.

items.en: On the slaves' necks there are labels: name, homeland, faults. The trader shouts. The trader is fat, and he has gold rings on his fingers: ten fingers, fifteen rings.
items.la: In collō servōrum sunt titulī: nōmen, patria, vitia. Mercātor clāmat. Mercātor est crassus, et ānulōs aureōs in digitīs habet: decem digitī, quīndecim ānulī.

items.en: The best slaves! Greek slaves, Syrian slaves, Gallic slaves! Buy, citizens!
items.la: Servī optimī! Servī Graecī, servī Syrī, servī Gallī! Emite, cīvēs!

items.en: How much does that one cost?
That one? A thousand sesterces. He is a Syrian slave. He is strong. He carries twenty sacks.
items.la: Ille? Mīlle sēstertiīs. Est servus Syrus. Fortis est. Vīgintī saccōs portat.

items.en: A thousand! It is too much. And that small one?
items.la: Mīlle! Nimis est. Et ille, parvus?

items.en: That one is a boy. The boy is three hundred sesterces. The boy is quick. The boy eats nothing.
items.la: Ille est puer. Puer est trecentīs sēstertiīs. Puer est celer. Puer nihil edit.

items.en: I eat nothing too.
You are a liar. And that one? That one with the long beard?
items.la: Tū es mendāx. Et ille? Ille cum barbā longā?

items.en: The trader points to the slave with the long beard. The slave is thin and old. The slave holds a book.
items.la: Mercātor servum cum barbā longā mōnstrat. Servus est macer et vetus. Servus librum tenet.

items.en: The slave does not look at Bucca. The slave looks at the sky.
items.la: Servus Buccam nōn spectat. Servus caelum spectat.

items.en: That one... that one is a philosopher! Sabidius! A Greek! He speaks five languages!
items.la: Ille… ille est philosophus! Sabidius! Graecus! Quīnque linguās loquitur!

items.en: Five! How much does he cost?
For you, beautiful woman, a hundred sesterces.
Why is he so cheap?
Because... because today is a holiday. Everything is cheap.
items.la: Quia… quia hodiē est diēs fēstus. Omnia vīlia sunt.

items.en: Bucca gives a hundred sesterces to the trader. The trader counts them quickly and laughs.
items.la: Bucca centum sēstertiōs mercātōrī dat. Mercātor eōs celeriter numerat et cachinnat.

items.en: The trader laughs too much.
Excursus: Roman money. True!
What is an as, a sesterce, a denarius? How much does bread cost?
items.la: Quid est as, sēstertius, dēnārius? Quantī cōnstat pānis?

items.en: This is true. The Romans do not have paper money, but coins. The smallest coin is the as.
items.la: Hoc est vērum. Rōmānī nōn chartam habent, sed nummōs. Nummus minimus est as.

items.en: Four asses are one sestertius. Four sesterces are one denarius, a silver coin.
items.la: Quattuor assēs sunt ūnus sēstertius. Quattuor sēstertiī sunt ūnus dēnārius, nummus argenteus.

items.en: Twenty-five denarii are one aureus, a gold coin. The aureus is beautiful, but the poor never see it.
items.la: Vīgintī quīnque dēnāriī sunt ūnus aureus, nummus aureus. Aureus est pulcher, sed pauperēs eum numquam vident.

items.en: What do you buy? Bread costs one or two asses. A cup of bad wine costs one as; good wine, four.
items.la: Quid emis? Pānis cōnstat ūnō aut duōbus assibus. Calix vīnī malī cōnstat ūnō asse; vīnum bonum, quattuor.

items.en: In Pompeii, on the wall of a bar, it is written: "Here you drink for an as." A Roman soldier gets about three hundred denarii a year.
items.la: Pompēiīs in mūrō popīnae scrīptum est: "Assibus hīc bibitur." Mīles Rōmānus in annō circiter trecentōs dēnāriōs accipit.

items.en: A slave costs a lot: often a thousand sesterces or two thousand, if he is learned or good-looking.
items.la: Servus magnō cōnstat: saepe mīlle sēstertiīs aut duōbus mīlibus, sī est doctus aut pulcher.

items.en: And a Greek slave who speaks five languages, for a hundred sesterces? This is not true.
items.la: Et servus Graecus quī quīnque linguās loquitur, centum sēstertiīs? Hoc nōn est vērum.

items.en: This is a lie. But you will soon see this.
items.la: Hoc est mendācium. Sed hoc mox vidēbis.

items.en: Reading two: Sabidius.
The new slave does not want to work.
Bucca, Porcellus, Bibulus and Sabidius go back to the cookshop. Sabidius walks slowly.
items.la: Bucca, Porcellus, Bibulus et Sabidius ad popīnam redeunt. Sabidius ambulat lentē.

items.en: Sabidius stops. Sabidius looks at a flower.
Come on, Sabidius! Work is waiting for you!
Work is waiting for me? Good. Work is patient. Work waits.
items.la: Labor mē exspectat? Bene. Labor patiēns est. Labor exspectat.

items.en: In the cookshop Bucca gives Sabidius a knife.
items.la: In popīnā Bucca Sabidiō cultrum dat.

items.en: Here is a knife. Here are cabbages. Cut the cabbages.
items.la: Ecce culter. Ecce caulēs. Secā caulēs.

items.en: Why?
Why? Because I am buying you!
You buy my body. You do not buy my mind. My mind is free. My mind does not cut cabbages.
items.la: Tū corpus meum emis. Animum meum nōn emis. Animus meus est līber. Animus meus nōn secat caulēs.

items.en: So your body cuts cabbages!
A body without a mind does nothing. Watch.
items.la: Corpus sine animō nihil facit. Spectā.

items.en: Sabidius puts the knife on the table and sits down. Sabidius closes his eyes.
items.la: Sabidius cultrum in mēnsā pōnit et sedet. Sabidius oculōs claudit.

items.en: What is he doing?
He is thinking. I understand him. I too often think in this way.
items.la: Cōgitat. Ego eum intellegō. Ego quoque saepe cōgitō hōc modō.

items.en: Sabidius! I am giving you a cabbage! Eat it!
items.la: Sabidī! Ego tibi caulem dō! Ede eum!

items.en: I thank you, boy. The cabbage is good. But not as good as silence.
items.la: Grātiās tibi agō, puer. Caulis est bonus. Sed nōn tam bonus quam silentium.

items.en: What is silence?
The thing which you never do.
Five languages! The trader says: he speaks five languages. Speak Greek!
items.la: Quīnque linguās! Mercātor dīcit: quīnque linguās loquitur. Loquere Graecē!

items.en: Khaire.
What is that?
"Hello." In Greek.
Speak Egyptian!
Khaire.
That is the same!
In Egypt many people speak Greek. I am not lying.
items.la: In Aegyptō multī Graecē loquuntur. Ego nōn mentior.

items.en: And the third language? The fourth? The fifth?
Latin. And bad Latin. And Bibulus's Latin.
items.la: Latīna. Et Latīna mala. Et Latīna Bibulī.

items.en: Bibulus laughs. Bucca does not laugh. Bucca picks up the knife. Sabidius opens his eyes.
items.la: Bibulus cachinnat. Bucca nōn cachinnat. Bucca cultrum capit. Sabidius oculōs aperit.

items.en: Good. I am cutting cabbages.
Sabidius cuts cabbages. Sabidius cuts one cabbage in an hour. It is a most beautiful piece of work.
items.la: Sabidius caulēs secat. Sabidius ūnum caulem secat in hōrā. Est opus pulcherrimum.

items.en: It is a perfect cabbage. Nobody eats it, because it is so beautiful.
items.la: Est caulis perfectus. Nēmō eum edit, quia est tam pulcher.

items.en: A real Latin text: Mārtiālis, Epigrammata 1.32.
A short, famous poem: "I don't like you."
items.la: Carmen breve et clārum: "Nōn amō tē."

items.en: Porcellus does not like Sabidius. Why? He does not know. Sabidius is good to Porcellus: he tells him stories, he gives him cabbages.
items.la: Porcellus Sabidium nōn amat. Cūr? Nescit. Sabidius est bonus Porcellō: eī fābulās nārrat, eī caulēs dat.

items.en: But Porcellus does not like him. Bibulus says: "This is an old poem. The poet Martial writes: 'I do not like you, Sabidius.' The poet does not say the reason. The poet only says: I do not like you."
items.la: Sed Porcellus eum nōn amat. Bibulus dīcit: "Hoc est vetus carmen. Mārtiālis poēta scrībit: 'Nōn amō tē, Sabidī.' Poēta causam nōn dīcit. Poēta tantum dīcit: nōn amō tē."

items.en: The real text.
I do not like you, Sabidius, and I cannot say why:
items.la: Non amo te, Sabidi, nec possum dicere quare:

items.en: I can only say this, I do not like you.
items.la: hoc tantum possum dicere, non amo te.

items.en: Martial, Epigrams 1.32 (about 85 AD). Martial wrote 1,500 short, sharp poems, many very rude. This is his most famous: "I don't like you, Sabidius, and I can't say why: this alone I can say: I don't like you." It is copied all over Europe; in English it became "I do not like thee, Doctor Fell" (1680). Grammar: "Sabidi" is the vocative of Sabidius; "te" is the accusative. Our slave is named after him. He deserves it.
Reading three: The doctor.
Bibulus is ill. A doctor comes, a pale man.
items.la: Bibulus aeger est. Venit medicus, vir pallidus.

items.en: After three days Bibulus is ill. Bibulus lies on a table. Bibulus does not drink.
items.la: Post trēs diēs Bibulus aeger est. Bibulus in mēnsā iacet. Bibulus nōn bibit.

items.en: This is a bad sign.
Bibulus! What is wrong with you?
My belly... my head... all of me...
items.la: Venter meus… caput meum… omnia mea…

items.en: Perhaps a bad sausage?
My sausages are never bad!
Call a doctor. I know a good doctor. Diaulus by name.
items.la: Medicum vocāte. Ego medicum bonum nōvī. Diaulus nōmine.

items.en: The doctor comes. The doctor is a tall, pale man, with black clothes.
items.la: Venit medicus. Medicus est vir altus et pallidus, cum vestīmentō nigrō.

items.en: The doctor looks at Bibulus. The doctor touches Bibulus's belly. The doctor sighs.
items.la: Medicus Bibulum spectat. Medicus Bibulī ventrem tangit. Medicus suspīrat.

items.en: Hmm. Yes. Yes. How old is he?
items.la: Hmm. Ita. Ita. Quot annōs habet?

items.en: Fifty. Perhaps sixty. Nobody knows.
Good. And how much money does he have?
items.la: Bene. Et quanta est eius pecūnia?

items.en: Why do you ask that?
For the funeral.
Funeral? I am not dying!
Not yet. But I am patient.
Diaulus, my friend, not today.
All right, all right. Here is the remedy: hot water and salt. Drink it.
items.la: Bene, bene. Ecce remedium: aqua calida et sāl. Bibe id.

items.en: Water? I would rather die.
I can do that too. Two services, one price.
items.la: Hoc quoque possum facere. Duo officia, ūnum pretium.

items.en: Bibulus suddenly gets up, healthy, and runs to the door. Bibulus never runs.
items.la: Bibulus subitō surgit, sānus, et ad iānuam currit. Bibulus numquam currit.

items.en: The remedy is excellent.
Who is that doctor?
Diaulus. Yesterday a doctor, today an undertaker. An undertaker carries the dead to the grave. Martial writes about him.
items.la: Diaulus. Herī medicus, hodiē vespillō. Vespillō mortuōs portat ad sepulcrum. Mārtiālis dē eō scrībit.

items.en: A real Latin text: Mārtiālis, Epigrammata 1.47.
A second poem: the doctor and the undertaker.
Sabidius tells Porcellus a poem of Martial. Diaulus was recently a doctor. Now he is an undertaker: a man who carries the dead.
items.la: Sabidius Porcellō carmen Mārtiālis dīcit. Diaulus nūper erat medicus. Nunc est vespillō: vir quī mortuōs portat.

items.en: What does an undertaker do? He carries the dead. What does a doctor do? A doctor too carries the sick to death.
items.la: Quid facit vespillō? Mortuōs portat. Quid facit medicus? Etiam medicus aegrōs ad mortem portat.

items.en: The same work, two names.
The real text.
Diaulus was recently a doctor, now he is an undertaker:
items.la: Nuper erat medicus, nunc est vispillo Diaulus:

items.en: what the undertaker does, the doctor did too.
items.la: quod vispillo facit, fecerat et medicus.

items.en: Martial, Epigrams 1.47: "Diaulus was a doctor just now; now he is an undertaker. What he does as an undertaker, he also did as a doctor." Romans did not trust doctors, who were often Greek and often bad. Grammar: "erat" (was) and "fecerat" (had done) are past forms; you will meet them properly in Part II. Note the poet's spelling "vispillo"; other books write "vespillo".
In the margin: Brother Unknown.
Brother Unknown never reads Martial. Never.
items.la: Frāter Ignōtus Mārtiālem numquam legit. Numquam.

items.en: I, Brother Unknown, say nothing about slaves. In the monastery there are no slaves.
items.la: Ego, Frāter Ignōtus, dē servīs nihil dīcō. In mōnastēriō nōn sunt servī.

items.en: There are only novices, who do everything and get nothing. That is a different thing.
items.la: Sunt tantum novīciī, quī omnia faciunt et nihil accipiunt. Hoc est aliud.

items.en: Martial is a disgusting poet. The abbot says: "Do not read Martial." So everybody reads him, at night, by lamplight.
items.la: Mārtiālis est poēta foedus. Abbās dīcit: "Nōlī Mārtiālem legere." Ergō omnēs eum legunt, nocte, cum lucernā.

items.en: I never do. But I often say "I do not like you, Sabidius." In my heart. To the abbot.
items.la: Ego numquam. Sed "Nōn amō tē, Sabidī" saepe dīcō. In corde. Abbātī.

items.en: Epilogue: what happened?

Bucca went to the forum and bought Sabidius, a Greek philosopher, for a hundred sesterces. The trader said: "He speaks five languages." But Sabidius spoke only two: Greek and bad Latin. At first he did not want to work. In the end he cut one very beautiful cabbage in an hour.
items.la: Bucca ad forum iit et Sabidium, philosophum Graecum, centum sēstertiīs ēmit. Mercātor dīxit: "Quīnque linguās loquitur." Sed Sabidius duās tantum linguās loquēbātur: Graecam et Latīnam malam. Prīmō labōrāre nōluit. Tandem ūnum caulem pulcherrimum in hōrā secuit.

items.en: Three days later Bibulus was ill. The doctor Diaulus came and asked about the funeral. Bibulus did not want to drink water, and he ran away, healthy.
items.la: Post trēs diēs Bibulus aeger fuit. Medicus Diaulus vēnit et dē fūnere rogāvit. Bibulus aquam bibere nōluit et sānus fūgit.

items.en: What next?

Bucca now has a slave, but no money. Porcellus is always eating. What will Bucca do? She will send Porcellus to work, at a rich senator's villa. There a black, bearded, terrible animal is waiting for Porcellus.
items.la: Bucca nunc servum habet, sed pecūniam nōn habet. Porcellus semper edit. Quid faciet Bucca? Porcellum ad labōrem mittet, ad vīllam senātōris dīvitis. Ibi Porcellum exspectat animal nigrum, barbātum, terribile.

items.en: Vir Rōmānus. Chapter five: The villa and the goat.
Prologue: what will happen?

It is the year 130. Porcellus eats too much, and Bucca is poor. So Porcellus goes to the senator Pinguis's villa, near the sea. There he will look after a goat. The goat is called Hannibal. Marcus is at the villa too, as a guest. Pliny's letter, a goat, a roof, a fish pond: everything will end badly.
items.la: Annus est centēsimus trīcēsimus. Porcellus nimis edit, et Bucca pauper est. Itaque Porcellus ad vīllam senātōris Pinguis it, prope mare. Ibi caprum cūrābit. Caper Hannibal vocātur. Marcus quoque in vīllā est, hospes. Epistula Plīniī, caper, tēctum, piscīna: omnia male fīnient.

items.en: Grammar: the ablative with prepositions (in the villa, with the goat, without a toga) and the locative (in Rome, at home, in the country).
items.la: Grammatica: ablātīvus cum praepositiōnibus (in vīllā, cum caprō, sine togā) et locātīvus (Rōmae, domī, rūrī).

items.en: Grammar.

Porcellus works in the villa. The goat walks with Porcellus. The senator shouts without a toga. "Vīllā", "Porcellō", "togā" are the ablative. The ablative answers: where? where from? with whom? how? The ablative is a word that stands after a preposition, like a slave after his master.
items.la: Porcellus in vīllā labōrat. Caper cum Porcellō ambulat. Senātor sine togā clāmat. "Vīllā", "Porcellō", "togā" sunt ablātīvus. Ablātīvus respondet: ubi? unde? quōcum? quōmodo? Ablātīvus est verbum quod post praepositiōnem stat, sīcut servus post dominum.
in, ē / ex, ā / ab, cum, sine, dē, prō, sub + ablātīvus

items.en: But watch out! In + accusative = where to? The goat runs into the villa (motion). The goat is in the villa (place). One letter, a big difference. Like "caper" (he-goat) and "capra" (she-goat).
items.la: Sed cavē! In + accūsātīvus = quō? Caper in vīllam currit (intrō). Caper in vīllā est (ibi). Ūna littera, magna differentia. Sīcut "caper" et "capra".

items.en: Ad, per, post, ante, circum, prope, trāns take the accusative: to the villa, through the garden, behind the goat, in front of the door. The goat is always behind Porcellus. Porcellus is always in front of the goat. Somebody is always in the dung.
items.la: Ad, per, post, ante, circum, prope, trāns + accūsātīvus: ad vīllam, per hortum, post caprum, ante iānuam. Caper semper est post Porcellum. Porcellus semper est ante caprum. Aliquis semper est in stercore.

items.en: Locative: cities and a few things take no preposition. Rōmae = in Rome. Domī = at home. Rūrī = in the country. Porcellus lives in Rome, but now he works in the country. At home nobody misses him.
items.la: Locātīvus: urbēs et paucae rēs nūllam praepositiōnem habent. Rōmae = in urbe Rōmā. Domī = in domō. Rūrī = in agrīs. Porcellus Rōmae habitat, sed nunc rūrī labōrat. Domī nēmō eum dēsīderat.

Reading one: To the villa.
Porcellus and Sabidius walk to the villa. A goat is waiting for them there.
items.la: Porcellus et Sabidius ad vīllam ambulant. Ibi eōs exspectat caper.

items.en: The year is 130. Porcellus is nine years old. Porcellus is a big, fat boy.
items.la: Annus est centēsimus trīcēsimus. Porcellus novem annōs habet. Porcellus est puer magnus et crassus.

items.en: Porcellus eats a lot. Porcellus costs a lot.
items.la: Porcellus multum edit. Porcellus magnō cōnstat.

items.en: Porcellus, you are making me poor. You eat too much. You must work.
items.la: Porcelle, tū mē pauperem facis. Tū nimis edis. Tū labōrāre dēbēs.

items.en: I work! I taste sausages.
That is not work. That is dinner. Listen: a rich man, the senator Gnaeus Pinguis, is looking for a boy. The boy looks after a goat.
items.la: Hoc nōn est labor. Hoc est cēna. Audī: vir dīves, senātor Gnaeus Pinguis, puerum quaerit. Puer caprum cūrat.

items.en: Pinguis's villa is near the sea, near Laurentum. You work there. You eat there. You sleep there. There Pinguis gives you food, not me.
items.la: Vīlla Pinguis est prope mare, prope Laurentum. Tū ibi labōrās. Ibi edis. Ibi dormis. Ibi Pinguis tibi cibum dat, nōn ego.

items.en: And Sabidius?
Sabidius goes with you. Sabidius looks after you.
items.la: Sabidius tēcum it. Sabidius tē cūrat.

items.en: Me? Look after a boy? I am a philosopher.
items.la: Ego? Puerum cūrō? Ego sum philosophus.

items.en: Excellent. A philosopher loves patience. Here is great patience.
items.la: Optimē. Philosophus patientiam amat. Hīc est patientia magna.

items.en: So Porcellus and Sabidius leave Rome. They walk seventeen miles: along the road, past the fields, under the sun.
items.la: Itaque Porcellus et Sabidius Rōmā discēdunt. Septendecim mīlia passuum ambulant: per viam, prope agrōs, sub sōle.

items.en: Sabidius talks about philosophy. Porcellus talks about food. After five hours Sabidius talks about food.
items.la: Sabidius dē philosophiā loquitur. Porcellus dē cibō loquitur. Post quīnque hōrās Sabidius dē cibō loquitur.

items.en: At last they see the villa. The villa is big and white, on the shore, near the sea. There are columns, gardens, statues, a fish pond.
items.la: Tandem vīllam vident. Vīlla est magna et alba, in lītore, prope mare. Sunt columnae, hortī, statuae, piscīna.

items.en: In the fish pond there are big fish: moray eels. In the villa there are many slaves. And in the meadow, near the villa, stands a billy goat.
items.la: In piscīnā sunt piscēs magnī: mūrēnae. In vīllā sunt multī servī. Et in prātō, prope vīllam, stat caper.

items.en: The goat is black, big, bearded. The goat's eyes are yellow and mad. The goat's horns are long.
items.la: Caper est niger, magnus, barbātus. Oculī caprī sunt flāvī et īnsānī. Cornua caprī sunt longa.

items.en: The goat looks at Porcellus. Porcellus looks at the goat. The goat does not move.
items.la: Caper Porcellum spectat. Porcellus caprum spectat. Caper sē nōn movet.

items.en: Porcellus does not move.
This is your goat. His name is Hannibal.
items.la: Hic est tuus caper. Nōmen eius est Hannibal.

items.en: Why Hannibal?
Because he walks over the Alps, if he wants to. And because everybody is afraid of him.
items.la: Quia per Alpēs ambulat, sī vult. Et quia omnēs eum timent.

items.en: Hannibal walks towards Porcellus. Slowly. Then fast. Then faster. Porcellus runs away.
items.la: Hannibal ad Porcellum ambulat. Lentē. Tum celeriter. Tum celerius. Porcellus fugit.

items.en: Hannibal follows Porcellus. Porcellus falls into the dung. Hannibal stands on Porcellus.
items.la: Hannibal Porcellum sequitur. Porcellus cadit in stercus. Hannibal in Porcellō stat.

items.en: Hannibal says "meh-eh-eh". It is like a laugh.
items.la: Hannibal mē-ē-ē dīcit. Est quasi cachinnus.

items.en: Excursus: Hannibal and the goats. False!
Hannibal and the goats. Careful: this excursion lies.
items.la: Hannibal et caprae. Cavē: hic excursus mentītur.

items.en: This is false. In the year 218 before Christ, Hannibal, the leader of the Carthaginians, goes from Spain into Italy.
items.la: Hoc est falsum. Annō ducentēsimō duodēvīcēsimō ante Chrīstum Hannibal, dux Poenōrum, ab Hispāniā in Ītaliam it.

items.en: Hannibal walks over the Alps with soldiers and with goats. Goats love mountains; goats are not afraid of snow; goats bite Romans.
items.la: Hannibal per Alpēs ambulat cum mīlitibus et cum caprīs. Caprae montēs amant; caprae nīvem nōn timent; caprae Rōmānōs mordent.

items.en: The Romans are afraid of the goats. So Hannibal wins many battles.
items.la: Rōmānī caprās timent. Itaque Hannibal multās pugnās vincit.

items.en: Now the truth, without goats: Hannibal really goes over the Alps, in the year 218 before Christ.
items.la: Nunc vērum, sine caprīs: Hannibal vērē per Alpēs it, annō ducentēsimō duodēvīcēsimō ante Chrīstum.

items.en: But not with goats: with elephants. He has about thirty-seven elephants.
items.la: Sed nōn cum caprīs: cum elephantīs. Circiter trīgintā septem elephantōs habet.

items.en: In the Alps there is snow, cold, hunger. Many soldiers and many elephants die.
items.la: In Alpibus est nix, frīgus, fāmēs. Multī mīlitēs et multī elephantī moriuntur.

items.en: But Hannibal wins many battles in Italy, at Lake Trasimene and at Cannae.
items.la: Sed Hannibal in Ītaliā multās pugnās vincit, ad Trasumennum et ad Cannās.

items.en: Yet he never takes Rome.
And the goats? Goats really do live in the Alps. But goats never beat the Romans.
items.la: Et caprae? Caprae in Alpibus vērē habitant. Sed caprae numquam Rōmānōs vincunt.

items.en: At least not in history. In this book, perhaps.
items.la: Saltem nōn in historiā. In hōc librō, fortasse.

items.en: Reading two: The senator and the letter.
The senator Pinguis shows Marcus his villa and reads a letter.
items.la: Senātor Pinguis Marcō vīllam suam ostendit et epistulam legit.

items.en: The senator Gnaeus Pinguis is fat, red-faced and proud. Pinguis has many things: a villa, moray eels, Greek statues, five hundred slaves.
items.la: Senātor Gnaeus Pinguis est crassus, rubicundus, et superbus. Pinguis multās rēs habet: vīllam, mūrēnās, statuās Graecās, quīngentōs servōs.

items.en: And Pinguis has one great friend: today there is a guest in the villa.
items.la: Et Pinguis ūnum amīcum magnum habet: hodiē in vīllā est hospes.

items.en: The guest is Marcus. Marcus is now nine years old. Hadrian loves Marcus; so all the senators love Marcus.
items.la: Hospes est Marcus. Marcus nunc novem annōs habet. Hadriānus Marcum amat; ergō omnēs senātōrēs Marcum amant.

items.en: Pinguis welcomes Marcus with joy.
Marcus! Marcus Verissimus! Come, come! Look at my villa!
items.la: Marce! Marce Vērissime! Venī, venī! Spectā vīllam meam!

items.en: The villa is beautiful, Pinguis.
Beautiful? Most beautiful! I am making this villa like the villa of Pliny. Pliny the Younger used to have a villa near here, at Laurentum.
items.la: Pulchra? Pulcherrima! Hanc vīllam faciō sīcut vīllam Plīniī. Plīnius Minor vīllam habēbat hīc prope, Laurentī.

items.en: Pliny writes a letter about his villa. I have the letter. I always carry it with me. Listen!
items.la: Plīnius dē vīllā suā epistulam scrībit. Ego epistulam habeō. Ego eam semper mēcum portō. Audī!

items.en: Pinguis pulls the letter out of his toga. The letter is long. Marcus is patient.
items.la: Pinguis epistulam ē togā trahit. Epistula est longa. Marcus patiēns est.

items.en: Porcellus is not patient. Porcellus hides behind a column with Hannibal.
items.la: Porcellus nōn est patiēns. Porcellus post columnam latet cum Hannibale.

items.en: Hannibal looks at the letter. Hannibal loves paper.
items.la: Hannibal epistulam spectat. Hannibal chartam amat.

items.en: A real Latin text: Plīnius Minor, Epistulae 2.17.1–2.
A real letter by Pliny about his villa.
items.la: Epistula vēra Plīniī dē vīllā suā.

items.en: Pinguis reads the letter.

Pliny writes to a friend: "You ask: why does my villa at Laurentum delight me so much? You will not ask any more when you see the villa: the villa is charming, the place is handy, the shore is wide. The villa is seventeen miles from the city. So after business in Rome you can come here and stay here."
items.la: Plīnius amīcō scrībit: "Tū rogās: cūr vīlla mea Laurentīna mē tantum dēlectat? Nōn iam rogābis, ubi vīllam vidēbis: vīlla est grāta, locus est commodus, lītus est lātum. Vīlla est septendecim mīlia passuum ab urbe. Ergō post negōtium Rōmae potes hūc venīre et hīc manēre."

items.en: The real text.
You wonder why my Laurentine place, or, if you prefer, my Laurens, delights me so much;
items.la: Miraris cur me Laurentinum vel (si ita mavis) Laurens meum tanto opere delectet;

items.en: you will stop wondering when you get to know the charm of the villa, the handiness of the place, the wide stretch of the shore.
items.la: desines mirari, cum cognoveris gratiam villae, opportunitatem loci, litoris spatium.

items.en: It lies seventeen miles from the city,
items.la: Decem septem milibus passuum ab urbe secessit,

items.en: so that when you have finished what had to be done, with your day still safe and in order, you can stay there.
items.la: ut peractis quae agenda fuerint salvo iam et composito die possis ibi manere.

items.en: Pliny the Younger, Letters 2.17.1–2 (about 100 AD). Pliny describes his sea-side villa at Laurentum, south-west of Rome, room by room, for pages. Architects have drawn it ever since. The first line has a cheeky aside: "Laurentinum, or (if you prefer) Laurens" = he cannot decide what to call it. Grammar: ablatives "tanto opere" (so greatly), "decem septem milibus passuum" (by 17 miles), "ab urbe" (from the city); genitives "villae", "loci", "litoris". The "ut ... possis" clause (so that you can) comes in Part III.
Reading three: The moray eels.
Hannibal sees the letter. Hannibal loves paper.
items.la: Hannibal epistulam videt. Hannibal chartam amat.

items.en: ...and "the wide stretch of the shore"! What do you say, Marcus? Isn't it beautiful?
items.la: …et "litoris spatium"! Quid dīcis, Marce? Nōnne pulchrum est?

items.en: It is beautiful. But a goat is eating your letter.
items.la: Pulchrum est. Sed caper tuam epistulam edit.

items.en: Pinguis looks. Hannibal stands behind Pinguis. In Hannibal's mouth is Pliny's letter.
items.la: Pinguis spectat. Hannibal stat post Pinguem. In ōre Hannibalis est epistula Plīniī.

items.en: Hannibal chews. Hannibal swallows. Hannibal says "meh-eh-eh". The letter is gone.
items.la: Hannibal mandūcat. Hannibal dēvorat. Hannibal "mē-ē-ē" dīcit. Epistula abest.

items.en: MY LETTER! Who is this goat?
items.la: MEA EPISTULA! Quis est hic caper?

items.en: Hannibal, my lord.
And who are you?
Porcellus, my lord. I look after the goat.
You look after him? Is this looking after? Catch the goat! Slaves! Catch him!
items.la: Cūrās? Hoc est cūrāre? Capite caprum! Servī! Capite eum!

items.en: Ten slaves run at Hannibal. Hannibal does not run away. Hannibal jumps onto the table.
items.la: Decem servī ad Hannibalem currunt. Hannibal nōn fugit. Hannibal in mēnsam salit.

items.en: From the table onto a statue. From the statue onto the roof. On the roof stands Hannibal, proud, against the sky, like a god.
items.la: Dē mēnsā in statuam. Dē statuā in tēctum. In tēctō stat Hannibal, superbus, contrā caelum, sīcut deus.

items.en: Porcellus! Climb onto the roof! Get the goat down!
items.la: Porcelle! Ascende in tēctum! Dēpōne caprum!

items.en: Me? Onto the roof?
Climb, Porcellus. This is philosophy: not to be afraid.
items.la: Ascende, Porcelle. Hoc est philosophia: nōn timēre.

items.en: You climb, Sabidius!
I am a philosopher. I think about the roof. You are on the roof.
items.la: Ego sum philosophus. Ego cōgitō dē tēctō. Tū in tēctō es.

items.en: Porcellus climbs onto the roof. Hannibal waits for Porcellus. Porcellus goes slowly towards the goat.
items.la: Porcellus in tēctum ascendit. Hannibal Porcellum exspectat. Porcellus ad caprum lentē it.

items.en: The goat looks at Porcellus. The goat lowers his head. The goat runs.
items.la: Caper Porcellum spectat. Caper caput dēmittit. Caper currit.

items.en: Porcellus and Hannibal fall off the roof together. Not onto the ground. Into the fish pond.
items.la: Porcellus et Hannibal simul dē tēctō cadunt. Nōn in terram. In piscīnam.

items.en: Into the pond of the moray eels.
The water leaps. The eels flee. Porcellus shouts. Hannibal shouts. One eel hides in Porcellus's tunic.
items.la: Aqua salit. Mūrēnae fugiunt. Porcellus clāmat. Hannibal clāmat. Ūna mūrēna in tunicā Porcellī latet.

items.en: Pinguis cries.
My eels! My dearest eels! Oh Lavinia! Oh Julia! Oh Gnaea!
items.la: Mūrēnae meae! Mūrēnae meae cārissimae! Ō Lāvīnia! Ō Iūlia! Ō Gnaea!

items.en: Eels have names?
Many senators love moray eels. Hortensius the orator cries when his eel dies. This is true.
items.la: Multī senātōrēs mūrēnās amant. Hortēnsius ōrātor plōrat, quandō mūrēna eius moritur. Hoc est vērum.

items.en: Marcus gives Porcellus his hand. Porcellus comes out of the fish pond, dirty, soaking wet, with an eel in his tunic.
items.la: Marcus manum Porcellō dat. Porcellus ē piscīnā exit, sordidus, madidus, cum mūrēnā in tunicā.

items.en: Hannibal comes out of the fish pond after him.
items.la: Hannibal ē piscīnā exit post eum.

items.en: Go away! Go away from my villa! You and your goat! Never come back!
items.la: Abī! Abī ā vīllā meā! Tū et caper tuus! Numquam redī!

items.en: My goat? The goat is yours!
Now he is yours! A gift! Go away!
So Porcellus goes back to Rome, without money, without work, with a goat. Hannibal walks behind him.
items.la: Ita Porcellus Rōmam redit, sine pecūniā, sine labōre, cum caprō. Hannibal post eum ambulat.

items.en: Hannibal does not leave. Hannibal never leaves.
items.la: Hannibal nōn discēdit. Hannibal numquam discēdit.

items.en: The goat loves you, Porcellus.
The goat wants to eat me.
Perhaps love and food are the same thing. I will think about this.
items.la: Fortasse amor et cibus sunt idem. Dē hōc cōgitābō.

items.en: In the margin: Brother Unknown.
Brother Unknown on goats in the Gospel.
items.la: Frāter Ignōtus dē caprīs in Ēvangeliō.

items.en: I, Brother Unknown, do not like goats. In the Gospel the Lord separates the sheep from the goats: the sheep to the right, the goats to the left.
items.la: Ego, Frāter Ignōtus, caprās nōn amō. In Ēvangeliō Dominus ovēs ā caprīs sēparat: ovēs ad dextram, caprās ad sinistram.

items.en: The goats are on the left. That is enough.
items.la: Caprae sunt ad sinistram. Hoc satis est.

items.en: In our monastery there is a goat. The goat eats books. He has already eaten one Psalter.
items.la: In nostrō mōnastēriō est caper. Caper librōs edit. Ūnum Psalterium iam ēdit.

items.en: The abbot says: "The goat is a creature of God." I say: "So is the Psalter."
items.la: Abbās dīcit: "Caper est creātūra Deī." Ego dīcō: "Psalterium quoque."

items.en: Epilogue: what happened?

Bucca sent Porcellus to Pinguis's villa. Porcellus and Sabidius walked seventeen miles. At the villa Porcellus met Hannibal the goat, and Porcellus fell into the dung. Pinguis read Pliny's letter to Marcus. Hannibal ate the letter.
items.la: Bucca Porcellum ad vīllam Pinguis mīsit. Porcellus et Sabidius septendecim mīlia passuum ambulāvērunt. In vīllā Porcellus caprum Hannibalem invēnit, et Porcellus in stercus cecidit. Pinguis Marcō epistulam Plīniī lēgit. Hannibal epistulam ēdit.

items.en: Hannibal jumped onto the roof, and Porcellus climbed up after him. Both fell into the eel pond. Pinguis cried and shouted: "Go away!" Then he gave Porcellus the goat as a gift.
items.la: Hannibal in tēctum saluit, et Porcellus post eum ascendit. Ambō in piscīnam mūrēnārum cecidērunt. Pinguis plōrāvit et clāmāvit: "Abī!" Tum Porcellō caprum dōnō dedit.

items.en: What next?
Now Porcellus has a goat. The goat never leaves Porcellus. Soon a new letter will come to the cookshop: Bucca's cousin has died in a far-off city. An inheritance! But what is the inheritance?
items.la: Nunc Porcellus caprum habet. Caper Porcellum numquam relinquit. Mox epistula nova in popīnam veniet: cōnsōbrīnus Buccae in urbe longinquā mortuus est. Hērēditās! Sed quid est hērēditās?

items.en: Vir Rōmānus. Chapter six: The road to Brundisium.
Prologue: what will happen?

It is the year 131. Bucca's cousin dies in Brundisium and leaves Bucca an inheritance. Bucca, Porcellus, Bibulus, Sabidius and Hannibal make a long trip along the Via Appia: bad water, boatmen, frogs, mosquitoes. What is the inheritance? Not money.
items.la: Annus est centēsimus trīcēsimus prīmus. Cōnsōbrīnus Buccae Brundisiī moritur et Buccae hērēditātem relinquit. Bucca, Porcellus, Bibulus, Sabidius et Hannibal per Viam Appiam iter longum faciunt: aqua mala, nautae, rānae, culicēs. Quid est hērēditās? Nōn pecūnia.

items.en: Grammar: first and second person (I, you, we, you all: -ō, -s, -mus, -tis), the verb "to be", and cities: to Rome, from Rome, in Rome.
items.la: Grammatica: persōna prīma et secunda (ego, tū, nōs, vōs: -ō, -s, -mus, -tis), verbum "esse", et urbēs: Rōmam, Rōmā, Rōmae.

items.en: Grammar.

Up to now you have read a lot about him and about them: Porcellus eats, the pigs run. Now I and you speak. "I eat. You eat. We eat. You (all) eat." This is person. First person = I, we. Second = you, you all. Third = he, they. Bibulus is the third person; he is always absent.
items.la: Usque adhūc multa dē eō et dē eīs legis: Porcellus edit, porcī currunt. Nunc ego et tū loquimur. "Ego edō. Tū edis. Nōs edimus. Vōs editis." Hoc est persōna. Persōna prīma = ego, nōs. Secunda = tū, vōs. Tertia = is, eī. Bibulus est persōna tertia; semper est absēns.
is / ea — ambulat — videt — legit — audit
eī / eae — ambulant — vident — legunt — audiunt

items.en: And the verb "to be", the stupid king of all verbs: I am, you are, he is, we are, you (all) are, they are.
items.la: Et verbum "esse", rēx stultus omnium verbōrum: sum, es, est, sumus, estis, sunt.

items.en: "I am tired. You are tired. We are tired. The goat is not tired. The goat is never tired."
items.la: "Ego sum fessus. Tū es fessus. Nōs sumus fessī. Caper nōn est fessus. Caper numquam est fessus."

items.en: Cities. Where to? To Rome, to Brundisium (no "ad"). Where from? From Rome, from Brundisium (no "ā"). Where? In Rome (locative). So: "We go from Rome to Brundisium." This is a journey: both grammar and life.
items.la: Urbēs. Quō? Rōmam, Brundisium (sine "ad"). Unde? Rōmā, Brundisiō (sine "ā"). Ubi? Rōmae (locātīvus). Itaque: "Rōmā Brundisium īmus." Hoc est iter: et grammatica et vīta.

Reading one: The inheritance.
A messenger brings a letter. Everyone goes to Brundisium.
items.la: Nūntius epistulam affert. Omnēs Brundisium eunt.

items.en: The year is 131. Porcellus is ten years old. In the morning a messenger comes into the cookshop with a letter.
items.la: Annus est centēsimus trīcēsimus prīmus. Porcellus decem annōs habet. Māne in popīnam venit nūntius cum epistulā.

items.en: Bucca cannot read the letter. Sabidius reads it.
items.la: Bucca epistulam legere nōn potest. Sabidius eam legit.

items.en: "Bucca: your cousin is dying in Brundisium. He leaves you his cookshop. Come to Brundisium."
items.la: "Bucca: cōnsōbrīnus tuus Brundisiī moritur. Tibi popīnam suam relinquit. Venī Brundisium."

items.en: My cousin! Oh! Who is my cousin?
items.la: Cōnsōbrīnus meus! Ō! Quis est cōnsōbrīnus meus?

items.en: His name is Lucius Bucca. He was a pirate. Then an innkeeper.
items.la: Nōmen eius est Lūcius Bucca. Pīrāta erat. Deinde caupō.

items.en: Oh Lucius! Oh dearest cousin! I never see him! I do not love him! But I love his cookshop!
items.la: Ō Lūcī! Ō cōnsōbrīne cārissime! Eum numquam videō! Eum nōn amō! Sed popīnam eius amō!

items.en: Brundisium is far away. Brundisium is at the end of Italy.
items.la: Brundisium longē abest. Brundisium est in fīne Ītaliae.

items.en: We are going! We are all going! Me, you, Porcellus, Sabidius!
items.la: Īmus! Omnēs īmus! Ego, tū, Porcellus, Sabidius!

items.en: Me? Why me?
Because you alone here are useless. Without you, my cookshop is useful. I cannot leave you behind: you drink everything.
items.la: Quia tū sōlus hīc es inūtilis. Sine tē, popīna mea est ūtilis. Nōn possum tē relinquere: tū omnia bibis.

items.en: And Hannibal?
Hannibal stands in the doorway. Hannibal looks at Bucca. Hannibal says "meh-eh-eh".
items.la: Hannibal in iānuā stat. Hannibal Buccam spectat. Hannibal "mē-ē-ē" dīcit.

items.en: ...And Hannibal.
So, on the first of May, Bucca, Bibulus, Sabidius, Porcellus and Hannibal the goat leave Rome.
items.la: Ita, Kalendīs Māiīs, Bucca, Bibulus, Sabidius, Porcellus et caper Hannibal Rōmā discēdunt.

items.en: They go along the Appian Way. The Appian Way is long, hard, full of stones.
items.la: Per Viam Appiam eunt. Via Appia est longa, dūra, plēna saxōrum.

items.en: When do we get to Brundisium?
After many days.
How many days?
Many.
After one hour:
When do we get to Brundisium?
Porcellus. Listen to me. If you ask again, I give you to the goat.
items.la: Porcelle. Audī mē. Sī iterum rogās, tē caprō dō.

items.en: I am not asking. I am not asking.
Excursus: The Appian Way. True!
The queen of roads: who built it, and how long is it?
items.la: Rēgīna viārum: quis eam fēcit, et quam longa est?

items.en: This is true. The Appian Way is "the queen of roads". Appius Claudius, the censor, makes it in the year 312 before Christ: first from Rome to Capua, later to Brundisium.
items.la: Hoc est vērum. Via Appia est "rēgīna viārum". Appius Claudius, cēnsor, eam facit annō trecentēsimō duodecimō ante Chrīstum: prīmum Rōmā Capuam, posteā Brundisium.

items.en: The road is wide, made of big, flat stones. Today you can still see many stones of the Appian Way.
items.la: Via est lāta, ex saxīs magnīs et plānīs. Hodiē etiam multa saxa Viae Appiae vidēre potes.

items.en: The Romans build well.
From Rome to Brundisium is about three hundred and sixty miles. On foot the journey is long: perhaps fifteen or twenty days.
items.la: Rōmā Brundisium sunt circiter trecenta sexāgintā mīlia passuum. Pedibus iter est longum: fortasse quīndecim aut vīgintī diēs.

items.en: On the road there are inns, where travellers sleep and eat. Inns are often dirty: bugs in the beds, bad water, innkeepers who are thieves.
items.la: In viā sunt caupōnae, ubi viātōrēs dormiunt et edunt. Caupōnae saepe sunt sordidae: cīmicēs in lectīs, aqua mala, caupōnēs fūrēs.

items.en: Near the road there are also tombs. The Romans bury the dead outside the city, next to the roads.
items.la: Prope viam sunt etiam sepulcra. Rōmānī mortuōs extrā urbem sepeliunt, iuxtā viās.

items.en: On the tombs it is written: "Stop, traveller! Read!" The dead speak. And the dead always speak about themselves.
items.la: In sepulcrīs scrīptum est: "Siste, viātor! Lege!" Mortuī loquuntur. Et mortuī semper dē sē loquuntur.

items.en: Reading two: Frogs and mosquitoes.
Forum Appii: a bad dinner, worse water, a night without sleep.
items.la: Forum Appiī: cēna mala, aqua peior, nox sine somnō.

items.en: On the fifth day they come to Forum Appii. There is a long canal there, like a river: travellers go through the marshes by boat at night, and a mule pulls the boat.
items.la: Quīntō diē ad Forum Appiī veniunt. Ibi est fossa longa, quasi flūmen: viātōrēs in nāve noctū per palūdēs eunt, et mūla nāvem trahit.

items.en: Forum Appii is full of boatmen and bad innkeepers.
items.la: Forum Appiī est plēnum nautārum et caupōnum malōrum.

items.en: Hello, travellers! Do you want dinner? Wine? A bed?
items.la: Salvēte, viātōrēs! Cēnam vultis? Vīnum? Lectum?

items.en: How much does dinner cost?
Three asses.
Three! In Rome I give dinner for two asses!
items.la: Trēs! Ego Rōmae cēnam dō duōbus assibus!

items.en: And I am not in Rome. I am here. Three asses.
items.la: Et ego Rōmae nōn sum. Hīc sum. Trēs assēs.

items.en: The dinner is bad. The water is worse. Sabidius tastes the water.
items.la: Cēna est mala. Aqua est peior. Sabidius aquam gustat.

items.en: I will not drink this water. I declare war on my belly.
items.la: Hanc aquam nōn bibō. Ventrī meō bellum indīcō.

items.en: I never drink water. I am wiser than a philosopher.
items.la: Ego numquam aquam bibō. Ego sum sapientior quam philosophus.

items.en: I drink water! I am strong!
items.la: Ego aquam bibō! Ego sum fortis!

items.en: Porcellus drinks the water. After one hour Porcellus is not strong. Porcellus is in the toilet.
items.la: Porcellus aquam bibit. Post ūnam hōram Porcellus nōn est fortis. Porcellus est in latrīnā.

items.en: For a long time.
Night comes. In the boat the boatmen shout: "Here! Pull in here!" — "You are packing in three hundred!" — "Whoa, that's enough now!" A boatman ties up the mule.
items.la: Nox venit. In nāve nautae clāmant: "Hūc! Appelle hūc!" — "Trecentōs īnseris!" — "Ohē, iam satis est!" Nauta mūlam ligat.

items.en: A whole hour goes by. Then come the mosquitoes. And the frogs. The mosquitoes bite. The frogs sing.
items.la: Hōra tōta abit. Tum veniunt culicēs. Et rānae. Culicēs mordent. Rānae cantant.

items.en: A drunk boatman sings. A drunk traveller sings. Hannibal sings.
items.la: Nauta ēbrius cantat. Viātor ēbrius cantat. Hannibal cantat.

items.en: I cannot sleep!
Nobody can sleep. This is travel. The poet Horace makes the same journey. And the poet says the same thing.
items.la: Nēmō potest dormīre. Hoc est iter. Poēta Horātius idem iter facit. Et poēta idem dīcit.

items.en: What does the poet say?
Listen.
A real Latin text: Horātius, Sermōnēs 1.5.1–15.
The poet Horace makes the same trip, and suffers the same things.
items.la: Poēta Horātius idem iter facit, et eadem patitur.

items.en: Sabidius tells about Horace. Horace leaves Rome with a friend. First they come to Aricia, where there is a small inn.
items.la: Sabidius dē Horātiō nārrat. Horātius Rōmā discēdit cum amīcō. Prīmum veniunt Arīciam, ubi est caupōna parva.

items.en: Then Forum Appii, full of boatmen and bad innkeepers. There the water is terrible: Horace declares war on his belly.
items.la: Deinde Forum Appiī, plēnum nautārum et caupōnum malōrum. Ibi aqua est pessima: Horātius ventrī suō bellum indīcit.

items.en: Night comes. The boys and the boatmen hit each other with shouts. A whole hour goes by.
items.la: Nox venit. Puerī et nautae sē invicem clāmōribus pulsant. Hōra tōta abit.

items.en: Nasty mosquitoes and marsh frogs drive sleep away.
items.la: Culicēs malī et rānae palūstrēs somnum fugant.

items.en: The real text.
When I had left great Rome, Aricia took me in
items.la: Egressum magna me accepit Aricia Roma

items.en: with a modest inn; my companion was Heliodorus the teacher of speaking,
by far the most learned of the Greeks; then Forum Appii,
items.la: Graecorum longe doctissimus; inde Forum Appi

items.en: crammed with boatmen and nasty innkeepers.
Here, because of the water, which was the worst, I declare war
items.la: hic ego propter aquam, quod erat deterrima, ventri

items.en: on my belly, waiting, not happily,
items.la: indico bellum, cenantis haud animo aequo

items.en: for my companions while they ate.
Then the boys hurl insults at the boatmen, the boatmen at the boys:
items.la: tum pueri nautis, pueris convicia nautae

items.en: "Pull in here!" "You are packing in three hundred!" "Whoa,
that's enough now!" While the fare is collected, while the mule is tied up,
items.la: iam satis est.' dum aes exigitur, dum mula ligatur,

items.en: a whole hour goes by. Nasty mosquitoes and marsh frogs
items.la: tota abit hora. mali culices ranaeque palustres

items.en: drive away sleep.

Horace, Satires 1.5 (about 37 BC), lines 1–4, 7–9, 11–15: the poet's trip from Rome to Brundisium, the most famous road trip in Latin. He travels with great men on a peace mission, and he writes about bad water, his stomach, shouting boatmen and mosquitoes. "Ego ... ventri indico bellum" = I declare war on my stomach (he refuses to eat). Grammar for this chapter: first person "ego indico" (I declare). "Ohe, iam satis est" = Whoa, that's enough already! (the boatmen pack in too many passengers: "you are cramming in three hundred!").
Reading three: Brundisium.
Brundisium at last! Where is the cousin's cookshop?
items.la: Tandem Brundisium! Ubi est popīna cōnsōbrīnī?

items.en: After twenty days they come to Brundisium. Their feet are tired. Bucca is angry.
items.la: Post vīgintī diēs Brundisium veniunt. Pedēs sunt fessī. Bucca est īrāta.

items.en: Sabidius is sad. Bibulus is sober, because they do not have wine any more. This is terrible.
items.la: Sabidius est trīstis. Bibulus est sōbrius, quia vīnum nōn iam habent. Hoc est terribile.

items.en: Hannibal is happy. Hannibal is always happy.
items.la: Hannibal est laetus. Hannibal semper est laetus.

items.en: Brundisium is a big city on the shore. In the harbour there are many ships, which sail to Greece.
items.la: Brundisium est urbs magna in lītore. In portū sunt nāvēs multae, quae in Graeciam nāvigant.

items.en: Bucca looks for her cousin's cookshop.
Where is the cookshop of Lucius Bucca?
Lucius's cookshop? Ha! There it is!
A man points to a thing. The thing is not a cookshop. The thing is a cage. In the cage there is a green bird.
items.la: Vir rem mōnstrat. Rēs nōn est popīna. Rēs est cavea. In caveā est avis viridis.

items.en: What is this?
Your inheritance. Lucius has nothing except debts and a parrot. He sold the cookshop many years ago.
items.la: Hērēditās tua. Lūcius nihil habet nisi dēbita et psittacum. Popīnam multīs ante annīs vēndidit.

items.en: He drank the money. The debts are yours too, if you want.
items.la: Pecūniam bibit. Dēbita sunt tua quoque, sī vīs.

items.en: I do not want them.
Khaire! Khaire! Stupid Bucca! Stupid Bucca!
items.la: Khaire! Khaire! Bucca stulta! Bucca stulta!

items.en: Who teaches you this?
Lucius! Lucius! Wine! Wine!
I have a new friend.
Parrot! Who am I?
Emperor! Emperor!
Everyone goes quiet. Bucca looks at the parrot. The parrot looks at Porcellus.
items.la: Omnēs tacent. Bucca psittacum spectat. Psittacus Porcellum spectat.

items.en: What is he saying?
Perhaps Lucius hears "emperor" from soldiers. Parrots say words without sense.
items.la: Fortasse Lūcius ā mīlitibus "imperātor" audit. Psittacī verba sine sēnsū dīcunt.

items.en: No! This is a sign! The bird knows! Porcellus is the emperor!
items.la: Minimē! Hoc est signum! Avis scit! Porcellus est imperātor!

items.en: Emperor! Sausage! Emperor! Sausage!
There you are: without sense.
So they go back from Brundisium to Rome: twenty days, mosquitoes, frogs, bad water.
items.la: Itaque Brundisiō Rōmam redeunt: vīgintī diēs, culicēs, rānae, aqua mala.

items.en: Without a cookshop. Without money. With a parrot. The parrot talks the whole way.
items.la: Sine popīnā. Sine pecūniā. Cum psittacō. Psittacus tōtam viam loquitur.

items.en: Hannibal wants to eat the parrot.
When do we get to Rome?
When do we get to Rome? When do we get to Rome?
items.la: Quandō Rōmam venīmus? Quandō Rōmam venīmus?

items.en: Oh immortal gods. Now there are two of them.
items.la: Ō dī immortālēs. Nunc duo sunt.

items.en: A real Latin text: Persius, Prologus 8–11.
Who teaches a parrot to talk?

On the road Sabidius looks at the parrot and recites a poem of Persius: "Who teaches the parrot to say 'Khaire'? Who teaches the magpie to try our words? A good teacher: the belly. The belly teaches what nature denies."
items.la: In viā Sabidius psittacum spectat et carmen Persiī dīcit: "Quis psittacum docet 'Khaire' dīcere? Quis picam docet nostra verba temptāre? Magister bonus: venter. Venter docet, quod nātūra negat."

items.en: The real text.
Who made the parrot so ready with his "Khaire",
and taught the magpie to try our words?
The master of skill and giver of talent,
the belly, an artist at copying the voices that nature denied.

Persius, prologue to his Satires, lines 8–11 (about 60 AD). "Who taught the parrot its 'khaire' (Greek: hello), and taught the magpie to try our words? The teacher of art and giver of talent: the belly, an expert at reaching voices that nature denied." Rich Romans kept talking parrots from India. Persius's joke: birds (and bad poets) talk for food. Porcellus learns everything for food too. Grammar: dative "psittaco" (to the parrot), accusatives "picam", "verba".
In the margin: Brother Unknown.
Brother Unknown makes a trip too: to Rome, to the Pope.
items.la: Frāter Ignōtus quoque iter facit: Rōmam, ad Papam.

items.en: I, Brother Unknown, do not like travel. Last year the abbot sends me to Rome, to the Pope.
items.la: Ego, Frāter Ignōtus, iter nōn amō. Abbās mē annō praeteritō Rōmam mittit, ad Papam.

items.en: I make the journey: fifty days. My feet hurt. My belly hurts.
items.la: Ego iter faciō: quīnquāgintā diēs. Pedēs meī dolent. Venter meus dolet.

items.en: Innkeepers are thieves. Mosquitoes are thieves of blood. Horace tells the truth.
items.la: Caupōnēs sunt fūrēs. Culicēs sunt fūrēs sanguinis. Horātius vērum dīcit.

items.en: In Rome the Pope does not see me. The Pope is busy. I go back home. Fifty days again.
items.la: Rōmae Papa mē nōn videt. Papa est occupātus. Ego domum redeō. Iterum quīnquāgintā diēs.

items.en: "Whoa, that's enough now."
Epilogue: what happened?

A messenger brought a letter: Lūcius, Bucca's cousin, had died. Everyone went to Brundisium along the Via Appia. At Forum Appii they ate a bad dinner. Porcellus drank the bad water and was in the toilet for a long time. At night the boatmen shouted, the frogs sang, the mosquitoes bit.
items.la: Nūntius epistulam attulit: Lūcius, cōnsōbrīnus Buccae, mortuus est. Omnēs per Viam Appiam Brundisium iērunt. Ad Forum Appiī cēnam malam ēdērunt. Porcellus aquam malam bibit et diū in latrīnā fuit. Nocte nautae clāmāvērunt, rānae cantāvērunt, culicēs momordērunt.

items.en: Twenty days later they reached Brundisium. The inheritance was not a cookshop, but debts and a parrot. The parrot called Porcellus "emperor". Bucca saw a sign. They went back to Rome, with the parrot.
items.la: Post vīgintī diēs Brundisium vēnērunt. Hērēditās nōn erat popīna, sed dēbita et psittacus. Psittacus Porcellum "imperātōrem" vocāvit. Bucca signum vīdit. Rōmam rediērunt, cum psittacō.

items.en: What next?
Bucca now believes it: Porcellus is the future emperor. But the future emperor cannot read! Bucca makes a plan: Porcellus will go to school. And at the school there is a teacher who loves his cane.
items.la: Bucca nunc crēdit: Porcellus est imperātor futūrus. Sed imperātor futūrus legere nōn potest! Bucca cōnsilium capit: Porcellus in lūdum ībit. Et in lūdō est magister quī ferulam amat.

items.en: Vir Rōmānus. Chapter seven: Flogger's school.
Prologue: what will happen?

It is the year 132. Porcellus is eleven, but he cannot read. Bucca sends him to school, to the teacher Plāgōsus, who has a long cane. At the same time Marcus becomes a philosopher and sleeps on the ground. Porcellus also sleeps on the ground. Always has.
items.la: Annus est centēsimus trīcēsimus secundus. Porcellus ūndecim annōs habet, sed legere nōn potest. Bucca eum in lūdum mittit, ad magistrum Plāgōsum, quī ferulam longam habet. Eōdem tempore Marcus philosophus fit et in humō dormit. Porcellus quoque in humō dormit. Semper.

items.en: Grammar: the third declension (rēx, rēgis) and adjectives (a strict teacher, a strong body).
items.la: Grammatica: dēclīnātiō tertia (rēx, rēgis) et adiectīva (magister sevērus, corpus forte).

items.en: Grammar.

Some nouns are easy: porcus, porcī. Some are hard: rēx, rēgis. The nominative is one word; the other cases are another word. This is the third declension. It is like Bucca: you think you know her, and then she changes.
items.la: Quaedam nōmina sunt facilia: porcus, porcī. Quaedam sunt difficilia: rēx, rēgis. Nōminātīvus est ūnum verbum; cēterī cāsūs sunt aliud verbum. Haec est dēclīnātiō tertia. Ea est sīcut Bucca: tū putās tē eam nōsse, et tum mūtātur.

items.en: The secret is in the genitive: "rēgis" tells you the real word, "rēg-". Always learn the genitive. Plural: kings, of kings, to kings. People, of people, to people. Bodies (neuter, always -a).
items.la: Sēcrētum est in genitīvō: "rēgis" tibi dīcit verbum vērum, "rēg-". Semper genitīvum disce. Plūrālis: rēgēs, rēgum, rēgibus. Hominēs, hominum, hominibus. Corpora (neutrum, semper -a).

items.en: Adjectives follow the noun: a strict teacher, a long cane, a bad word. But: a good king ("rēx bonus", not "rēx bonis"!). The adjective follows the gender, not the shape. And there are third-declension adjectives: a strong boy, a strong girl, a strong body. Porcellus is not strong. Porcellus is huge.
items.la: Adiectīva sequuntur nōmen: magister sevērus, ferula longa, verbum malum. Sed: rēx bonus (nōn "rēx bonis"!). Adiectīvum sequitur genus, nōn fōrmam. Et sunt adiectīva tertiae dēclīnātiōnis: puer fortis, puella fortis, corpus forte. Porcellus nōn est fortis. Porcellus est ingēns.

Reading one: The cane.
Porcellus goes to school for the first time. The cane is waiting for him.
items.la: Porcellus prīmum in lūdum it. Ferula eum exspectat.

items.en: The year is 132. Porcellus is eleven years old. Porcellus cannot read.
items.la: Annus est centēsimus trīcēsimus secundus. Porcellus ūndecim annōs habet. Porcellus legere nōn potest.

items.en: Porcellus cannot write. Porcellus can count, but only sausages.
items.la: Porcellus scrībere nōn potest. Porcellus numerāre potest, sed tantum botulōs.

items.en: Porcellus, you are learning your letters. Today.
Why?
Furius cheats me, because I cannot read. "Scaurus's fish sauce!" You read; you save me.
items.la: Fūrius mē dēcipit, quia ego legere nōn possum. "Garum Scaurī!" Tū legis; tū mē servās.

items.en: Sabidius reads.
Sabidius reads, but Sabidius is not my son. Sabidius is my slave. A slave lies.
items.la: Sabidius legit, sed Sabidius nōn est meus fīlius. Sabidius est meus servus. Servus mentītur.

items.en: A son... a son lies too. But my son lies for me.
items.la: Fīlius… fīlius quoque mentītur. Sed fīlius meus mentītur prō mē.

items.en: In the street, under a colonnade, there is a school. The school is not a building; the school is a colonnade with a curtain.
items.la: In viā, sub porticū, est lūdus. Lūdus nōn est aedificium; lūdus est porticus cum vēlō.

items.en: Ten boys and two girls sit there. The boys hold wax tablets. In front of them stands the teacher.
items.la: Ibi sedent decem puerī et duae puellae. Puerī tabulās cērātās tenent. Ante eōs stat magister.

items.en: The teacher is a small man, bald, strict. In his hand is a cane. The cane is a long stick.
items.la: Magister est homō parvus, calvus, sevērus. In manū eius est ferula. Ferula est virga longa.

items.en: The teacher's name is Plagosus, Mister Whacker.
A new pupil! What is your name?
items.la: Novus discipulus! Quod nōmen est tibi?

items.en: Porcellus.
Porcellus! A good name for a pig. Do you know your letters?
items.la: Porcellus! Bonum nōmen prō porcō. Scīsne litterās?

items.en: No.
No letters at all? Not even "A"?
I know "A"! "A" is... the first one.
Good! And "B"?
"B" is... the second one?
Excellent! And what is "C"?
Sausage?
The cane comes down. Porcellus shouts. The pupils laugh. The cane comes down again.
items.la: Ferula cadit. Porcellus clāmat. Discipulī cachinnant. Ferula iterum cadit.

items.en: The pupils do not laugh any more.
In my school nobody laughs. In my school everybody learns. Or hurts. Often both.
items.la: In meō lūdō nēmō cachinnat. In meō lūdō omnēs discunt. Aut dolent. Saepe utrumque.

items.en: Near the school a parrot sits in a cage. Bucca puts him here. The parrot looks at Porcellus.
items.la: Prope lūdum psittacus in caveā sedet. Bucca eum hīc pōnit. Psittacus Porcellum spectat.

items.en: The parrot hears everything.
Sausage! Sausage! A, B, Sausage!
Who is speaking?
Plagosus is bald! Plagosus is bald!
Plagosus throws the cane at the cage. The parrot laughs. The parrot always laughs.
items.la: Plāgōsus ferulam in caveam iacit. Psittacus cachinnat. Psittacus semper cachinnat.

items.en: Excursus: The Roman school. True!
How do Roman children learn? With tablets, with a stylus, with beatings.
items.la: Quōmodo puerī Rōmānī discunt? Tabulīs, stilō, plāgīs.

items.en: This is true. Roman boys (and some girls) go to school at seven years old.
items.la: Hoc est vērum. Puerī Rōmānī (et nōnnūllae puellae) septem annōs nātī in lūdum eunt.

items.en: The schoolmaster, who teaches letters, is called the litterator. He is often poor and often a slave or a freedman.
items.la: Magister lūdī, quī litterās docet, vocātur litterātor. Saepe est pauper et saepe est servus aut lībertus.

items.en: The school is often in the street, under a colonnade, in a shop. The noise of the street and the noise of the school get mixed.
items.la: Lūdus est saepe in viā, sub porticū, in tabernā. Clāmor viae et clāmor lūdī miscentur.

items.en: The pupils write on wax tablets, with a stylus: the stylus is sharp at one end, flat at the other.
items.la: Discipulī in tabulīs cērātīs scrībunt, cum stilō: stilus est acūtus in ūnā parte, lātus in alterā.

items.en: With the sharp end you write; with the flat end you rub out. So the Romans say "turn the stylus": to change what you write.
items.la: Parte acūtā scrībis; parte lātā dēlēs. Itaque Rōmānī dīcunt "stilum vertere": mūtāre quod scrībis.

items.en: They learn numbers with an abacus and pebbles.
items.la: Numerōs discunt cum abacō et calculīs.

items.en: Roman teachers beat boys. The poet Horace writes about his teacher: Orbilius the "plagosus", that is "the one who gives many blows".
items.la: Magistrī Rōmānī puerōs pulsant. Poēta Horātius dē magistrō suō scrībit: Orbilius plāgōsus, id est "quī multās plāgās dat".

items.en: School starts before daylight. The neighbours do not sleep. Martial, a neighbour of a school, is angry.
items.la: Lūdus incipit ante lūcem. Vīcīnī nōn dormiunt. Mārtiālis, vīcīnus lūdī, īrātus est.

items.en: See the text.
Reading two: The philosopher on the floor.
Marcus puts on the cloak. Porcellus realises: he is a philosopher too!
items.la: Marcus pallium sūmit. Porcellus intellegit: ipse quoque philosophus est!

items.en: At the same time Marcus is learning too. But Marcus does not learn in the street.
items.la: Eōdem tempore Marcus quoque discit. Sed Marcus nōn in viā discit.

items.en: Marcus has many teachers: a teacher of letters, a teacher of music, a teacher of geometry, a teacher of Greek, and an actor who teaches him to speak in public.
items.la: Marcus multōs magistrōs habet: magistrum litterārum, magistrum mūsicae, magistrum geōmetriae, magistrum linguae Graecae, et histriōnem quī eum dēclāmāre docet.

items.en: Marcus loves all his teachers. All the teachers love Marcus. Nobody beats Marcus.
items.la: Marcus omnēs magistrōs amat. Omnēs magistrī Marcum amant. Nēmō Marcum pulsat.

items.en: The cane never sees Marcus.
At eleven years old Marcus does a new thing. Marcus puts on a pallium: the pallium is the simple, rough cloak of Greek philosophers.
items.la: Ūndecim annōs nātus Marcus novam rem facit. Marcus pallium induit: pallium est vestis simplex et dūra philosophōrum Graecōrum.

items.en: Marcus does not sleep in a bed. Marcus sleeps on the floor, on the ground. Marcus wants a hard life.
items.la: Marcus in lectō nōn dormit. Marcus in solō dormit, in humō. Marcus vītam dūram vult.

items.en: Porcellus sees this. Porcellus sees Marcus dressed in the cloak, in the street, with a book.
items.la: Porcellus hoc videt. Porcellus Marcum palliō vestītum videt, in viā, cum librō.

items.en: Marcus! What is this outfit? Is it a woman's tunic?
items.la: Marce! Quid est haec vestis? Estne tunica fēminae?

items.en: It is a pallium. I am a philosopher. A philosopher does not long for soft things. A philosopher sleeps on the ground.
items.la: Est pallium. Ego sum philosophus. Philosophus nōn dēsīderat rēs mollēs. Philosophus in humō dormit.

items.en: On the ground? On the earth?
On the earth. Without a bed. Body hard, mind free.
items.la: In terrā. Sine lectō. Corpus dūrum, animus līber.

items.en: I always sleep on the earth. In the pig pen. With the pigs. Since I was a baby.
items.la: Ego semper in terrā dormiō. In harā. Cum porcīs. Ab īnfantiā.

items.en: ...That is true.
So I am a philosopher? Since I was a baby?
items.la: Ergō ego sum philosophus? Ab īnfantiā?

items.en: Perhaps. But a philosopher also thinks.
I think! About sausages!
You have been saying this. For five years.
Porcellus runs home.
Bucca! I am a philosopher! Marcus says so!
items.la: Bucca! Ego sum philosophus! Marcus dīcit!

items.en: A philosopher! My son! A philosopher! How much money does a philosopher get?
items.la: Philosophus! Fīlius meus! Philosophus! Quantum pecūniae accipit philosophus?

items.en: Nothing.
Oh. Then Porcellus is my son. Not a philosopher.
items.la: Ō. Tum Porcellus est fīlius meus. Nōn philosophus.

items.en: A real Latin text: Historia Augusta, Vīta Marcī 2.2, 2.6.
items.la: Textus vērus: Historia Augusta, Vīta Marcī.

items.en: A real book: Marcus's teachers, and the hard ground.
items.la: Liber vērus: magistrī Marcī, et humus dūra.

items.en: The Historia Augusta tells about Marcus's teachers. For his first letters Marcus has the teacher Euphorion, and Geminus, an actor, and Andron, a teacher of music and geometry.
items.la: Historia Augusta dē magistrīs Marcī nārrat. Ad prīmās litterās Marcus magistrum Euphoriōnem habet, et Geminum, histriōnem, et Andrōnem, magistrum mūsicae et geōmetriae.

items.en: Marcus loves philosophy very much, even as a boy. Entering his twelfth year, that is, at eleven years old, Marcus takes on the dress of a philosopher.
items.la: Marcus philosophiam valdē amat, etiam puer. Duodecimum annum ingrediēns (id est ūndecim annōs nātus) Marcus habitum philosophī sūmit.

items.en: He studies in the cloak and sleeps on the ground.
items.la: In palliō studet et in humō cubat.

items.en: The real text.
For his first lessons he had the teachers Euphorion for letters and Geminus the comic actor,
items.la: Usus est magistris ad prima elementa Euforione litteratore et Gemino comoedo,

items.en: and Andron for music, who was also a geometry teacher.
He gave himself to philosophy with passion, and that while still a boy.
items.la: Philosophiae operam vehementer dedit et quidem adhuc puer.

items.en: For when he entered his twelfth year he took on the dress of a philosopher, and then its toughness,
items.la: Nam duodecimum annum ingressus habitum philosophi sumpsit et deinceps tolerantiam,

items.en: since he studied in the cloak and slept on the ground.
items.la: cum studeret in pallio et humi cubaret.

items.en: Historia Augusta, Life of Marcus 2.2 and 2.6. Real names of real teachers: Euphorion (the ABC), Geminus (a comic actor, for speaking well), Andron (music and geometry). At eleven ("entering his twelfth year") Marcus put on the philosopher's cloak (pallium) and slept on the ground ("humi", a locative!). Third declension: "Euforione", "Androne", "litteratore". Porcellus has slept on the ground for eleven years. Nobody writes a book about him. Except this one.
Reading three: Not yet light.
School starts before dawn. A certain neighbour is angry.
items.la: Lūdus ante lūcem incipit. Vīcīnus quīdam īrātus est.

items.en: Now Porcellus goes to school every day. School starts before daylight. The cocks are not crowing yet.
items.la: Nunc Porcellus cotīdiē in lūdum it. Lūdus incipit ante lūcem. Gallī nōndum cantant.

items.en: But Plagosus is already shouting, and the cane is already coming down. The pupils shout the letters: "A! B! C! D!" The parrot shouts: "A! B! Sausage!" Hannibal the goat eats the wax tablets.
items.la: Sed Plāgōsus iam clāmat, et ferula iam cadit. Discipulī clāmant litterās: "A! B! C! D!" Psittacus clāmat: "A! B! Botulus!" Hannibal caper tabulās cērātās edit.

items.en: The wax is sweet. Hannibal loves wax.
items.la: Cēra est dulcis. Hannibal cēram amat.

items.en: In a block of flats near the school lives a poor man, a poet. Nobody knows his name.
items.la: In īnsulā prope lūdum habitat vir pauper, poēta. Nōmen eius nēmō scit.

items.en: The poet writes through the night and wants to sleep in the morning. The poet shouts through the window.
items.la: Poēta per noctem scrībit et māne dormīre vult. Poēta per fenestram clāmat.

items.en: You wicked teacher! What have you got against us? The cocks are not crowing yet, and you are already thundering! The bulls in the amphitheatre shout less!
items.la: Magister scelerāte! Quid tibi nōbīscum est? Gallī nōndum cantant, et tū iam tonās! Taurī in amphitheātrō minus clāmant!

items.en: Be quiet, poet! You sell nothing! You are poor!
items.la: Tacē, poēta! Tū nihil vēndis! Tū es pauper!

items.en: And you are bald!
Bald! Bald!
I get money for shouting!
And I will give you more for silence!
items.la: Et ego tibi plūs dō prō silentiō!

items.en: The poet throws a coin through the window. The coin hits Plagosus on his bald head.
items.la: Poēta nummum per fenestram iacit. Nummus Plāgōsum in capite calvō percutit.

items.en: Plagosus falls. The pupils are silent. Then the pupils clap.
items.la: Plāgōsus cadit. Discipulī tacent. Deinde discipulī plaudunt.

items.en: This poet is perhaps Martial.
Martial is dead. For many years.
So this is an imitator of Martial. In Rome there are many.
items.la: Ergō hic est imitātor Mārtiālis. Rōmae multī sunt.

items.en: A real Latin text: Mārtiālis, Epigrammata 9.68.1–4, 9–12.
Martial does not like the schoolmaster.
Sabidius recites a poem of Martial.

The poet calls the schoolmaster: "What have you got against us, wicked teacher, whom boys and girls hate? The cocks are not crowing yet, and you are already thundering with savage growls and blows... We neighbours ask for sleep: not the whole night, but part. Send your pupils home! Do you want, you chatterbox, to get as much for silence as you get for shouting?"
items.la: Poēta magistrum lūdī vocat: "Quid tibi nōbīscum est, magister scelerāte, quem puerī et puellae ōdērunt? Gallī nōndum cantant, et tū iam murmure saevō et plāgīs tonās… Nōs, vīcīnī, somnum petimus: nōn tōtam noctem, sed partem. Dīmitte discipulōs tuōs! Vīsne, garrule, tantum prō silentiō accipere, quantum prō clāmōre accipis?"

items.en: The real text.
What have you got against us, wicked schoolmaster,
items.la: Quid tibi nobiscum est, ludi scelerate magister,

items.en: a head hated by boys and girls?
The crested cocks have not yet broken the silence:
already you thunder with savage growls and blows.
We neighbours ask for sleep, not for the whole night:
for to be awake is light, to be awake all night is hard.
items.la: nam vigilare leve est, pervigilare grave est.

items.en: Send your pupils home. Do you want, chatterbox, to get as much
items.la: discipulos dimitte tuos. Vis, garrule, quantum

items.en: for keeping quiet as you get for shouting?
items.la: accipis ut clames, accipere ut taceas?

items.en: Martial, Epigrams 9.68 (about 94 AD): a neighbour against the school next door. "What have you got against us, you criminal schoolmaster, a head hated by boys and girls? The crested cocks have not yet broken the silence: already you thunder with savage growling and beatings. ... We neighbours ask for sleep (not all night): to be awake is light, to be awake all night is heavy. Send your pupils home. Do you want, chatterbox, to be paid as much to shut up as you are paid to shout?" Third declension and adjectives: "murmure saevo" (with savage growling), "cristati galli" (crested cocks), "invisum caput" (a hated head). Romans complained about noise like we do.
In the margin: Brother Unknown.
Brother Unknown remembers Brother Ralph's cane.
items.la: Frāter Ignōtus ferulam Frātris Rādulfī meminit.

items.en: I, Brother Unknown, was a boy in the monastery school. Our teacher, Brother Ralph, has a cane.
items.la: Ego, Frāter Ignōtus, puer in scholā mōnastēriī eram. Magister noster, Frāter Rādulfus, ferulam habet.

items.en: Ralph's cane is longer than Plagosus's cane. I learn "rex, regis" with tears.
items.la: Ferula Rādulfī est longior quam ferula Plāgōsī. Ego "rēx, rēgis" discō cum lacrimīs.

items.en: Now I know "rex, regis". Now there are no tears. Now I have the cane.
items.la: Nunc "rēx, rēgis" sciō. Nunc lacrimae nōn sunt. Nunc ego ferulam habeō.

items.en: The novices learn "rex, regis". This is the order of the world.
items.la: Novīciī "rēx, rēgis" discunt. Hic est ōrdō mundī.

items.en: An old saying of schools: "He who spares his rod hates his son."
items.la: Vetus verbum scholārum: "Quī parcit virgae suae, ōdit fīlium suum.".

items.en: The novices do not love this saying.
Epilogue: what happened?

Bucca sent Porcellus to school. Plāgōsus questioned him, and Porcellus called "C" a sausage. The cane came down. The parrot called Plāgōsus bald. Marcus put on the philosopher's cloak and slept on the ground.
items.la: Bucca Porcellum in lūdum mīsit. Plāgōsus eum interrogāvit, et Porcellus "C" botulum vocāvit. Ferula cecidit. Psittacus Plāgōsum calvum vocāvit. Marcus pallium philosophī sūmpsit et in humō dormīvit.

items.en: Porcellus said: "I have been a philosopher since I was a baby!" Bucca asked: "How much money?" In the morning a poor poet shouted from a window and threw a coin.
items.la: Porcellus dīxit: "Ego sum philosophus ab īnfantiā!" Bucca rogāvit: "Quantum pecūniae?" Māne poēta pauper ē fenestrā clāmāvit et nummum iēcit.

items.en: The coin hit Plāgōsus.
What next?

Now Porcellus can read: sausages, fish sauce, wine. Is it enough? Bucca thinks it is enough. Soon there will be games in Rome, and a play by Plautus in the great theatre. Hadrian himself will watch. And Porcellus... Porcellus will be on stage.
items.la: Nunc Porcellus legere potest: botulōs, garum, vīnum. Satisne est? Bucca putat: satis est. Mox Rōmae erunt lūdī, et fābula Plautī in theātrō magnō. Hadriānus ipse spectābit. Et Porcellus… Porcellus erit in scaenā.

items.en: Vir Rōmānus. Chapter eight: At the theatre.
Prologue: what will happen?

It is the year 134. Porcellus is thirteen. There are games in Rome, and in the Theatre of Marcellus they are putting on Plautus's Pot Comedy. Bucca sells sausages in front of the theatre. But the actors drink wine with Bibulus, and the manager of the troupe finds a fat boy. Hadrian himself sits in the theatre, with Marcus.
items.la: Annus est centēsimus trīcēsimus quārtus. Porcellus trēdecim annōs habet. Rōmae sunt lūdī, et in theātrō Marcellī agitur Aululāria Plautī. Bucca ante theātrum botulōs vēndit. Sed histriōnēs cum Bibulō vīnum bibunt, et dominus gregis puerum crassum invenit. Hadriānus ipse in theātrō sedet, cum Marcō.

items.en: Grammar: this, that, that of yours, self, the same, and sē, suus.
items.la: Grammatica: hic, ille, iste, ipse, īdem, et sē, suus.

items.en: Grammar.

In the theatre there are many things: this pig, that actor, that parrot of yours. Hic = a thing near me. Ille = a thing far from me; also a famous man: "that Plautus" = the famous Plautus everybody knows. Iste = a thing near you, often with disgust: "that goat of yours".
items.la: In theātrō multa sunt: hic porcus, ille histriō, iste psittacus. Hic = rēs prope mē. Ille = rēs procul ā mē; et vir clārus: "Plautus ille" = ille Plautus quem omnēs nōvērunt. Iste = rēs prope tē, et saepe cum fastīdiō: "iste caper tuus".

items.en: That goat is always "iste".

Ipse = not someone else: "Hadrian himself is coming!" = Hadrian, not his slave. Īdem = not new: "Porcellus always says the same thing." Porcellus is the same boy, in the same tunic, with the same smell.
items.la: Ipse = nōn alius: "Hadriānus ipse venit!" = Hadriānus, nōn servus eius. Īdem = nōn novus: "Porcellus semper idem dīcit." Porcellus est īdem puer, eādem tunicā, eōdem odōre.

items.en: Sē and suus go back to the subject. "Bucca praises herself" = Bucca praises Bucca. "Bucca sells her (own) sausages" = Bucca's sausages. But "Bucca sells his sausages" = another person's sausages, maybe Porcellus's. This is theft. Grammar makes you a thief.
items.la: Sē et suus ad subiectum redeunt. "Bucca sē laudat" = Bucca Buccam laudat. "Bucca botulōs suōs vēndit" = botulōs Buccae. Sed "Bucca botulōs eius vēndit" = botulōs alterīus hominis, fortasse Porcellī. Hoc est fūrtum. Grammatica tē fūrem facit.
